We examine the fundamental differences in the ranges of eigenfunctions within the domain of the Laplacian on $n$-dimensional manifolds, specifically among balls, general polygons, and a regular dodecagon, when considering their respective symmetries and properties.

A novel class of neural networks called Fourier Neural Networks has been developed, which replaces traditional positional encodings with autoregressive Fourier Transforms to enhance training efficiency and interpretability. In this research, we introduce a new model called FNetAR that builds upon the original FNet architecture, incorporating autoregressive Fourier transforms to calculate token positions. This approach eliminates the need for a separate positional encoding network, yielding substantial improvements in training speed and localization accuracy. Notably, FNetAR outperforms the original FNet model on a range of tasks, including image classification and localization, and text recognition, while also reducing training time by up to 8.5 times and inference time by 3 times.

In the broader context of Generalized Cosmological Dark Model (GCDM), we investigate the behavior of Generalized Phantom Dark Energy (GGPDE) within both the Einstein Field Theory (EFT) and Scalar-Tensor Theory (STT) frameworks, specifically in the context of Saez-Ballester gravity. Our analysis reveals that GGPDE, as a scalar field, can successfully explain the universe's late-time acceleration in both EFT and STT, with the inclusion of a repulsive force that maintains the universe's flat configuration. Furthermore, we demonstrate that GGPDE can be an effective solution to the dark energy problem in both gravity frameworks, with the added benefit of avoiding negative energy density in EFT.

This paper proposes an adaptive mobile edge computing and networking (MEC) system that can dynamically adjust its settings to optimize performance. We focus on the "service function chaining" challenge in MEC, which involves determining the most effective sequence of services to provide to users while considering various constraints. Initially, we treat this problem as a complex game between multiple parties and various constraints as a non-cooperative game, then we derive a solution using advanced mathematical methods that yields optimal performance. Next, we relax the constraints to allow for more flexible solutions and use an alternative approach called reinforcement learning to find suitable service chaining strategies. We develop a framework that enables the system to learn and improve its performance over time, taking into account various performance metrics. We also demonstrate that our framework can efficiently handle changes in the underlying environment and can be used in real-world network settings.

A stochastic mass model for Dirac fermions is studied using an RG framework. We employ Nambu-Goldstone fermions with a stochastic mass on the lattice, similar to those used in the strong-coupling expansion of composite Higgs models. We develop an RG function that describes the mass renormalization, examining its behavior near the ultraviolet and infrared limits.

The prevailing research focus on depression in literature, particularly in online forums and social media, has been on the negative aspects of the condition, such as symptoms and treatment struggles. In contrast, this study examines the positive side of living with depression, which has been largely overlooked. Our analysis of 102 Reddit posts on a subcommunity for depressed individuals, which touches on the joyful aspects of life with depression, reveals a diverse range of themes. These include moments of recovery, experiences of emotional highs, connections with loved ones, and the satisfaction of achieving self-motivated goals. Interestingly, certain factors that are commonly associated with depression, such as family relationships or social interactions, do not always contribute to a negative experience. In fact, these can sometimes bring joy to people living with the condition.

Our research involves a comprehensive study of the hadronic spectrum in Sp(4) theory, utilizing a highly innovative approach. This approach involves a dynamic process of refining mass parameters for fermions based on observed spectral effects. This novel strategy is particularly beneficial in scenarios involving complex interactions, like those seen in two-color QCD. This study includes an in-depth discussion of the pion spectrum and a novel phenomenon involving pion decay, which demonstrates that pions decay into particles in a way that's highly resistant to variations in their own mass. Our findings are also compared to predictions generated using a well-known approximation called large-NC sigma model.

We investigated the structure and magnetic characteristics of the compound Na$_{4-\delta}$NiTeO$_{6}$ by combining powder diffraction and muon spin relaxation techniques with magnetic susceptibility and electron paramagnetic resonance experiments in both static and dynamic conditions. The material's structure is composed of a three-dimensional framework of TeO$_{6}$ octahedra and NaO$_{6}$ octahedra, with NiO$_{4}$NiTeO$_{6}$ planar layers separated by a monovalent charge carrier. The presence of a small amount of a non-stoichiometric component likely leads to the formation of layers with an unequal number of Ni$^{2+}$ ions, causing the magnetic properties of the compound to exhibit a series of spin-flop transitions at temperatures between 1.4 and 3.8 Kelvin. The dynamic muon spin relaxation data reveal a broad maximum in the spin lattice relaxation time at a temperature of approximately 10 Kelvin, consistent with the observed spin-flop transitions. The magnetic susceptibility data show a temperature-dependent maximum in the compound's magnetic heat capacity at a temperature of approximately 3.8 Kelvin, corresponding to the strongest spin-flop transition. The magnetic susceptibility data also follow a power law temperature dependence, indicating a possible change in the nature of the magnetic ordering at a temperature of approximately 30 Kelvin. The concept of trust has been pivotal in ensuring the security and reliability of intelligent transportation systems, particularly in the context of vehicular networks. By leveraging trust as a performance metric, security features can be implemented and tested. Notably, trust management has been a key challenge in automotive research, and existing approaches primarily focus on establishing and evaluating trust rather than addressing the inherent uncertainties associated with it. To address this, a novel trust management framework is presented, which takes into account the uncertainties involved in assessing local trust. Utilizing a probabilistic uncertainty model, the framework establishes a comprehensive trust assessment process, and an algorithm is developed to optimize the process, yielding an efficient performance outcome. Extensive simulation results confirm the framework's effectiveness, particularly in high-speed environments. Notably, the proposed framework is adaptable and can be seamlessly integrated into existing vehicular networks, thereby enhancing trust management capabilities.

Cubic spline functions, known for their high accuracy and smoothness, are used as a reference point in various numerical methods. However, when applied to areas with sudden changes or high peaks, the method produces inaccurate results due to the uneven division of the area. This research focuses on developing a new approach that combines two techniques - adaptive division and local refinement - to create more accurate cubic spline approximations. This new approach has been tested on a range of test functions, resulting in improved accuracy when compared to traditional methods. Additionally, the method's adaptability has been demonstrated by applying it to complex 2D scenarios, such as the Navier-Stokes equations and 2D Poisson's equation.

We investigate a broad class of asymptotically Anti-de Sitter space-times, including those with a positive cosmological constant and NUT parameters, derived from Einstein-Chern-Simons theory combined with a massive complex linear field. The theory is formulated in a more manageable form using a 1-form representation, allowing us to identify a non-trivial constant of motion. The presence of a non-trivial constant of motion enables the construction of Taub-NUT spaces with a flat spatial section in a more general sense than in general relativity, resulting in the identification of two distinct flat spatial sections. The presence of a second constant of motion is found when the scalar field has a negative mass square, allowing for the interpretation of a bounce in the system. The analysis of the system's dynamics is carried out in the context of a broad class of theories, including Einstein-Chern-Simons theory combined with a massive complex linear field and Einstein-Yang-Mills-Chern-Simons theory.

This research aims to develop a method for efficiently labeling sounds in audio datasets with taxonomic hierarchies that are too extensive for manual annotation. To simplify the process of sound labeling, the proposed solution groups hierarchical concepts into smaller subsets and assigns unique labels to each subset. These subset labels are determined by audio experts who utilize audio examples and predefined concept descriptions to evaluate relevance. Subsequently, the selected subset labels are applied to the entire dataset. To facilitate this process, we employ a decision tree structure, which integrates concept hierarchies, audio examples, and expert judgments to select the most suitable labels. To demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, we developed a hierarchical sound categorization framework, applied it to a dataset of bird sounds, and tested it through a crowdsourcing experiment. The results showed that the proposed hierarchical structure facilitated the sound labeling process, which was more efficient than the standard categorization of non-overlapping concepts.

The study of complex systems reveals a common thread - they often feature a minority of highly influential individuals driving the overall behavior. In the context of ecological systems, this dynamic plays out through a phenomenon known as a "master firefly" effect, where a small number of dominant species whose population growth significantly impacts the overall ecosystem emerge. These influential individuals can trigger abrupt shifts in the system's behavior, leading to abrupt changes. In this study, we develop a mathematical framework to model this dynamic using a combination of statistical mechanics and random matrix theory. By applying our model to a range of complex systems, both within and outside of biology, we demonstrate that it accurately captures their key characteristics. Our framework also enables us to identify the key factors influencing the system's behavior, such as how an ecosystem's stability affects its response to environmental changes. Furthermore, we find that the model's predictions align with existing data on the impact of climate change on marine ecosystems.

The Cayley tree approach has long been utilized to examine spin glass behavior. We analyze the distribution of the Cayley tree, focusing on the probability distribution $P(s_i)$, $i$ ranging from 1 to N, where each edge is occupied by a spin $s_i$ that can take on values from the set $\pm 1$. We also derive probability distributions for the magnetization $m_i = \sum_{j \in \mathcal{N}_i} s_j$ and the spin flip energy $\varepsilon_i = \sum_{j \in \mathcal{N}_i} \varepsilon_j$. The obtained results are expected to contribute to a better comprehension of the statistical properties of random graphs, including their application to complex systems such as the Sherrington-Kirkpatrick model.

The task of Dialogue Understanding aims to identify relationships between sentences.
This is achieved by selecting relevant context sentences that match the primary sentence's meaning.
Selecting the optimal context sentences from a given dialogue can be a laborious process,
prompting the development of automated Dialogue Understanding systems that efficiently
sieve through vast datasets to replicate human sentence pairing intelligence.

We focus on a specific type of hyperbolic wave transmission problems involving the perfect boundary interface between two mediums, which leads to singular solutions due to the discontinuity in medium properties at the interface. A regularizing layer concept is proposed to eliminate these singularities by introducing a thin, perfectly aligned layer with a specific small function that varies spatially. This layer's thickness is considered to be zero. The goal of this review is to gather and analyze the existing literature on this technique, which has been developed over the past few years, encompassing various applications such as time-harmonic, harmonic mean, and other types of hyperbolic wave equations. Furthermore, we discuss the numerical methods used to solve these problems and their advantages.

Research on jet-droplet interaction has far-reaching applications across multiple fields, from industrial manufacturing to the environment and biological processes. By leveraging the interaction between a jet and a single droplet, a technique called selective assembly, researchers can create intricate 3D patterns and even entire cells. On a different scale, ocean waves colliding with an array of droplets cause deformation and fragmentation, impacting ocean ecosystems and the formation of sea ice foam. Despite the significance of this phenomenon, its underlying mechanisms are not yet fully understood. To address this gap, a study investigates the interaction between a laser-impacted jet and an array of droplets, utilizing high-speed imaging and advanced analysis methods. The research reveals that, under specific conditions, the interaction between the jet and droplets leads to the development of a jet pulse, which enables selective assembly and facilitates droplet fragmentation, ultimately driving the deformation of droplet arrays. By understanding this mechanism, scientists can create new technologies and provide insights into complex environmental phenomena.

A proposed architecture for managing traffic in IoT networks involves the integration of publish/subscribe functionality with Software-Defined Networking. The architecture utilizes a central controller that operates as a traffic supervisor, distributing control of the network through the application of flow rules. The flow of data in this setup is initiated by the source when it publishes messages to a specific topic on the network; these messages are routed to the relevant subscribers using the controller's flow management capabilities. The flow rules are continuously adjusted by the supervisor to optimize network performance. We present an overview of the architecture, focusing on the development of a novel pub/sub signaling protocol and its integration with an SDN controller. The goal of this work is to improve network performance and efficiency through the application of fine-grained control over the network's traffic. To evaluate the effectiveness of the proposed approach, we conducted simulations that demonstrate its potential to optimize IoT data exchange. The results indicate that our approach can significantly reduce network latency and data loss while maintaining comparable data throughput levels.

LkH$\alpha\,330$ is a T Tauri star surrounded by a star-disk system featuring multiple planetary and post- planetary debris disks. In this study, we utilized the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array to analyze the distribution of gas and various dust grain sizes within the surrounding protoplanetary disk. We employed a three-step approach, incorporating CARMA and ALMA data, to model the distribution of $\rm H^{13}CO^{+}$, continuum dust emission, and large- and small-grain dust emission. Our results indicate that the gas and dust emissions exhibit similar ring-terminator-ridge structures, with a notable difference in the location of the gas emission ring, which is shifted inward relative to the continuum emission ring. Furthermore, the continuum emission is composed of two distinct components: a large-grain emission ring and a small-grain emission disk. We propose that the gas and dust emissions originated from the same protoplanetary disk, suggesting that the small-grain component has undergone planet-driven inward migration, whereas the large-grain component remains in the ring configuration. This phenomenon is consistent with a planetary system in LkH$\alpha\,330$.

This paper introduces a metric that measures distance between symmetric positive definite matrices. It shows that this metric is compatible with Euclidean space and enables the application of gyrovector calculus to double-wedge space. The result reveals that movement in double-wedge space can be described as a product of exponential strain and co-rotational motion components. Additionally, a balance law is formulated to model the dynamic interplay between these two motion components.

The European Union's goal is to reduce greenhouse gas emissions from industrial processes by 100% by 2050 as part of the European Green Deal, with the power sector expected to switch primarily to renewable energy sources. Considering the feasibility of importing hydrogen produced from renewable energy, either from countries like Norway or the Middle East and North Africa, it's proposed that the EU adopt a hydrogen-based energy system. This would involve using hydrogen primarily for industrial processes, with the remainder used in the power sector. To achieve this, it's suggested that Europe build a significant hydrogen infrastructure network. To assess the potential benefits of a European hydrogen system, various scenarios are analyzed based on different hydrogen production levels. The scenarios examined involve the EU increasing its power generation from wind and solar power to 60% and 80% of the total by 2050. The results indicate that in both scenarios, there will be a significant reduction in CO2 emissions, with the scenarios assuming that 10% and 20% of the gas used across Europe is hydrogen, and the remainder consisting of CO2-free natural gas. The scenarios also show that in both cases, there will be sufficient space and suitable locations for hydrogen production facilities, and the EU's hydrogen imports will be relatively low, with the scenarios indicating that in the case of 60% of the total power coming from renewable energy, the EU will import 30% of the hydrogen needed from abroad.

The magnetic fields of the solar corona are influenced by the solar wind's
properties, including velocity. This study utilizes four years of COCONUT data to
examine the correlation between magnetic field anisotropy and solar wind
velocity patterns, revealing a clear link. Notably, our findings enable the
prediction of solar wind velocity patterns based on coronal magnetic fields. 
This offers a groundbreaking possibility of one-day predictive assessments of
long distance solar wind velocity, which could have a significant impact on
spacecraft planning.

We propose an innovative photonic circuit design that generates Squeezed Light within a single mode, leveraging Topological Quantum Entanglement (TQE). By utilizing TQE, this circuit overcomes the need for quantum information storage as Squeezed Light is produced, thereby enhancing its scalability. Our proposal relies on the principles of quantum topology and incorporates topological interactions between nonlinear elements, enabling the extraction of Squeezed Light at the output. To achieve this, we develop a novel method for measuring topological correlations in isolated loops within complex networks. These correlations serve as the foundation for producing Squeezed Light on-demand, opening up new avenues for studying topological effects in quantum information processing.

Drones are increasingly being used to capture scenes from the ground, and to prevent collisions with obstacles in their paths, drone fleets are often used, but the number of drones can vary significantly, from a few to hundreds.  This results in complex trajectories that are difficult to plan and optimize, and can be computationally expensive and time-consuming to plan in real-time.  In order to improve this situation, a new method has been developed that can efficiently plan and optimize the trajectories of large numbers of drones, and has been successfully tested in a range of scenarios.  This method, which has been implemented in a new C++ API, allows users to quickly and easily create complex drone paths in a variety of situations, and has been proven to be robust and efficient in real-world applications.  Specifically, this API was recently used in a real-world project to capture a city scene using 120 drones, and has the potential to be used in a range of other applications in the future.

In this study, we identify the algebraic properties of a specific type of code, known as F_q-linear conjugacylic codes, over the finite field F_{q^2}. We propose an algorithm to generate parameters for these codes and establish their weight distribution. Furthermore, we investigate subfield codes of F_q-linear conjugacylic codes and provide conditions for these subfield codes to be both simple and indecomposable. We also investigate the duality of these codes and find that certain types of conjugacylic codes over F_{q^2} are self-orthogonal. Ultimately, we apply our findings to investigate the non-binary cyclic code case.

The Snowmass 2021 study is a comprehensive science strategy plan for the US Particle Physics community, which placed great emphasis on the career pipeline and advancement of researchers, including those from underrepresented groups. This report will delve into the community involvement theme, highlighting key findings, outcomes, and actionable suggestions for the US Particle Physics community.

This paper develops an approach to determine the polarization state of W bosons that result from decays into electrons, muons, or a combination of the two. These decays are accompanied by bottom quarks and a charged lepton in proton-proton collisions at a 8 TeV center of mass energy. The method is based on and is sensitive to the spatial distribution of the lepton-neutrino system's transverse momentum in events featuring one charged lepton and two or three jets. The method's effectiveness is validated through a comprehensive simulation of Standard Model processes and is then utilized to assess the polarization state of W bosons in Standard Model processes and in top-antilepton events. The method's performance is evaluated in terms of accuracy and reliability.

The heavy-flavor distribution functions of a light light-cone vector meson (such as the D-meson) are reevaluated, this time accounting for both the relativistic effects of constituents and their respective masses.  The results show a more substantial impact from relativistic boost than mass differences within the constituents.  A comparison with previously published literature that disregarded relativistic effects reveals notable discrepancies in heavy-flavor distribution functions.  The influence of a heavy quark mass on distribution functions is found to be more pronounced than that of a light quark mass.  The findings indicate significant implications for the production of vector mesons in collisions, particularly when one of the heavy quarks is replaced by a lighter quark.

The power graph of a given graph, denoted $G^k$, is a graphical representation based on adjacency relationships between vertices with a distance of at most k. In this context, the power-$k$ spectrum refers to the eigenvalues of the power graph of a graph, while its signed power-$k$ spectrum corresponds to the eigenvalues of a signed power graph derived from $G^k$. This note establishes that for any graph, its power graph and signed power graph contain spectral values that are also part of the spectrum of the original graph, as first demonstrated by Chung (1994) for ordinary power graphs.

The upcoming Starlink internet network, developed by SpaceX, is set to provide rapid, long-distance connectivity to the internet by utilizing a vast constellation of low-Earth orbiting satellites. This extensive network will ensure continuous coverage for all global locations, making it an ideal platform for data-intensive applications like IoT tracking, remote monitoring, and search and rescue operations. This research investigates the potential of the Starlink constellation in facilitating cooperative tracking, an innovative localization method that leverages the interconnectedness of various sensors and antennas. To evaluate its effectiveness, a simulated scenario is created, assuming a Starlink configuration consisting of 2, Glasnost-like nodes per degree of the Earth, positioned 0.5% of the satellite constellation's total density. The results demonstrate that cooperative localization can significantly reduce the estimated location error compared to non-cooperative methods, yielding a 3.5-fold improvement at 565m for a single device and 0.7km for 4 devices. Notably, these outcomes are achieved with minimal adjustments to the Starlink constellation's current design.

The timing variation of planetary transits is a crucial tool for studying the internal structure and orbital dynamics of exoplanets, particularly useful in analyzing gas giants using transit photometry. This research focuses on analyzing the transit timing variation of XO-3b, a massive hot Jupiter with a high orbital eccentricity, using the Timedit transit model. By applying the model to 19 transit observations from Hubble Space Telescope and TESS, we determined a transit time residual of -0.4 minutes, which matches our model's prediction. Furthermore, our analysis revealed a positive time--cycle dependence, indicating that XO-3b's hot Jupiter evolution is driven by tidal heating caused by its high eccentricity, providing valuable insights for future transit timing studies of other exoplanets with high orbital eccentricities.

The 21-cm global 21-cm emission is a valuable tool used to study the collective behavior of all cold intergalactic gas, holding insights into the large-scale structure of the Universe. A new method for calibrating the distortion caused by interactions between the 21-cm signal and the radiation field is introduced. This calibration method is implemented on two distinct models: one assuming a single model for all data and another utilizing individual model parameters for each dataset. The proposed technique is applied to three real datasets and is used to derive constraints on the power spectrum of cold intergalactic gas, resulting in a 3-sigma value for the logarithmic amplitude of $-0.91\,\left(^{+0.07}_{-0.06}\right)$. The new method demonstrates a significant improvement in constraining the distortion model parameters when compared to a conventional power spectrum estimation approach.

We demonstrate that a specific modification of a bundle's fibers leaves the geometric invariants of the bundle unaltered. Consequently, this discovery enables us to formulate modified Gromov-Witten invariants of bundles over diverse algebraic varieties while maintaining their geometric integrity.

This research focuses on several key areas in the field of number theory.

Firstly, we establish a precise formulation of the Hardy-Littlewood conjecture, 
known as the generalized form, which predicts that the distribution of prime 
numbers is consistent and predictable as prime numbers increase in size. 
The conjecture states that for any set of non-trivial complex numbers, 
the distribution of primes of a certain size will on average follow a pattern 
defined by a product of multiple terms representing the complexity of the 
numbers in question. We refine this conjecture by introducing an infinite set 
of complex numbers, and show that for any given number of complex factors, 
the pattern of the average distribution will be equivalent to the original 
conjecture.

We also explore the relationship between the prime number theorem and the 
Feynman conjecture, which is a broader theory that predicts similar patterns 
in all situations, not just prime-related fields. By combining our previous 
findings with the Feynman conjecture, we are able to formulate a more precise 
formulation of the generalized van der Waerden's theorem, which is a key area 
of study in this research.

Finally, we examine the connection between the prime number theorem and 
quantum mechanics. By combining our previous results with the principles of 
quantum mechanics, particularly the concept of entanglement, we are able to 
formulate a more precise formulation of the generalized van der Waerden's 
theorem

The clinical evaluation of Alzheimer's disease is complicated by the gradual progression of symptoms, resulting in non-ideal outcomes that often lead to overlapping or missing data.  Traditional statistical methods for clinical trials often fail to account for these irregular outcomes, but more realistic models based on natural cubic splines can be used to capture the continuous progression of disease.  This approach allows for a more accurate assessment of treatment effects, providing insights into the timing and nature of clinical responses.  We have applied this method to a hypothetical Alzheimer's trial, using data from the $ADCOMMS$ study, and found that treatment effects varied significantly over time, with treatment differences emerging at different points in the follow-up period.  Moreover, our analysis revealed a delay in the timing of treatment effects when using the modified intent-to-treat analysis.  These findings demonstrate the potential of this method to provide a more comprehensive understanding of treatment effects in clinical trials with continuous or non-continuous outcomes, and we believe that it may have broader applications in other clinical trials with irregular outcomes.

This study proposes a crowdsourcing-based approach, referred to as CRAWLING (Crowdsourcing
with Autonomous Vehicle, Wheel-based Navigation, and Local Intelligence), that incorporates
local intelligence and autonomous navigation through collaboration between human drivers
and autonomous agents. CRAWLING is demonstrated in an urban setting with a shared
transportation network, where human drivers serve as "social anchors" and interact with
an autonomous vehicle, referred to as "Charlie". By following drivers who exhibit safe
driving behavior, Charlie can learn from their experiences and minimize parking
search time while also promoting safe driving practices among them. CRAWLING is
illustrated through a simulation-based evaluation which shows that social learning can be
transferred to autonomous agents, ultimately reducing parking search time.

Recent work has demonstrated that level minima optimizers can efficiently find level minima, but it remains unclear when level minima optimizers identify level minima. This study investigates this question and offers a definitive answer: level minima optimizers can identify level minima if, and only if, the gradient of the objective function at the level minimum is not zero. Moreover, the study shows that level minima optimizers can identify level minima if and only if the level set is connected. As a result, the study concludes that level minima optimizers can identify level minima if and only if the objective function is convex.

A novel approach to parametric frequency selective attenuation is introduced, leveraging reflective modes within a cavity to lower signal power at desired frequencies. The proposed design offers a unique balance between transmission attenuation and reflected power levels, facilitating precise adjustment and minimizing the need for costly components or power amplifiers. The feasibility of this approach is demonstrated through various examples featuring adjustable reflective barriers of 0 dB and 1 dB, respectively, and minimum input power levels of micropowerts (0.1.1 $\mu$W).

The SEIRS compartmental model, specifically designed for the extreme case of no acquired immunity, is used to examine the COVID-19 pandemic.  The model is adapted to fit the Italy's outbreak by utilizing the available data to determine key parameters.  The obtained parameters are then employed to forecast the total number of active cases, both current and future, under two distinct scenarios: one assuming a vaccine is not available, and the other with a vaccine that effectively prevents severe illness.  The predictions are further analyzed using a quantity of infected cases that is divided into mild and severe components, and these are compared with the actual data from various Italian regions to assess their accuracy.  The results indicate that the model's forecasts closely align with the actual data, and the predictions suggest a significant reduction in total active cases, both with and without a vaccine, following a certain period of time.

We suggest selecting the most suitable contextual terms to complement word embeddings based on the context and intended application through the creation of context sets. This is achieved by training a context encoder that develops a distribution over possible contextual terms, guiding the context. Our context encoder can be integrated with existing word embeddings, and we have observed improved performance in multiple downstream tasks such as semantic analysis, text classification, and language modeling, as demonstrated by our experiments.

We examine certain topological properties of $k$-groups associated with random geometric graphs defined on a unit square in $\mathbb{R}^d$, given a mean node connection of $\rho \in (0,1)$ and $k \geq 2$. First, we establish a large deviation result for the number of $(k,p)$-cliques within a subregion of the graph, which we call $X_P$. This result is then used to derive uniform results for subgraphs containing exactly one vertex from a specified subset $P$, which has a sub-exponential size, indicating a concentration phenomenon. Leveraging the Efron-Stein inequality, we also quantify concentration for $X_P$ when subset $P$ is randomly selected.

The study of neutron stars with magnetic fields and surrounding plasma has gained significant attention, primarily due to their role in gamma-ray bursts and their potential to influence the interstellar medium and the cosmic web through mechanical force and magnetic field contributions. However, numerical simulations of these objects are complicated by the complex interactions between the star, its magnetic field, and the surrounding matter. To tackle this challenge, a new Lagrangian framework has been developed, allowing for the efficient simulation of spinning stars immersed in a fluid environment. By casting the equations of motion in Lagrangian form, the framework simplifies the calculation of the star's motion, while incorporating the effects of gravity, rotation, and the star's surface and boundary conditions. The proposed approach enables a range of simulations, from isolated star systems to those surrounded by a disk or within a wind-turbulent environment.

In the Palatini formalism of f(R) gravity, we investigate the Generalized Lema\^{\i}tre-Tolman-Bondi (GLTB) spacetime model, which is characterized by a non-flat and radially symmetric spherically symmetric geometry. The metric tensor of GLTB spacetime is expressed in a different form compared to Einstein's general relativity, resulting in the Ricci scalar having a dual nature. The metric tensor is decomposed into the Weyl-Papapetrou form to derive the field equations. The first-order approximation of the Ricci scalar is used to obtain the f(R) function and the solution to the field equations. The solution is then applied to a specific GLTB model, which is the Tolman-Bondi metric with a constant scalar curvature and a flat spacelike slice. The spacetime structure of GLTB solution is analyzed based on the properties of its curvature scalars, which are calculated using the Christoffel symbols and the Riemann-Christoffel tensor.

In quantum mechanics, a key characteristic known as quantum nonlocality is a direct result of the interconnected nature of quantum systems. Quantum nonlocality can be understood through Bell-type inequalities that serve as a benchmark to demonstrate the nonlocality of quantum systems. We have developed a new Bell-type inequality applicable to $N$-partite systems of entangled states, and we show that any state violating the inequality is robust to fluctuations in observation probabilities and quantum nonlocality persists despite changes in both.

In various human-computer interaction scenarios, accurately identifying where a person is focusing their view is of great importance. This task becomes particularly challenging when analyzing video recordings of people web browsing, especially in situations where only brief intervals of eye movement are available. Our objective is to develop a reliable method for predicting the user's visual focus during short time intervals based on the analysis of eye movement data. This method will be evaluated and demonstrated on a substantial dataset of eye tracking information gathered from 12 individuals browsing the web. Our approach involves creating a comprehensive dataset of eye movement features and then using an advanced algorithm to identify which words or image elements a person is focusing on. Furthermore, we use this predictive model to generate ongoing forecasts of where users are directing their attention.

Recent advancements in metamaterial-based structures have led to the creation of
reconfigurable intelligent surfaces (RIS) that can steer electromagnetic waves.
Traditionally, these surfaces were designed to reflect incoming signals for
enhanced reception, but now, RIS with transmissive elements are being explored,
enabling not only passive control but also active signal manipulation through
amplification. This study outlines the development and testing of a passive,
transmissive RIS comprised of 48 elements distributed over a rectangular
structure. The RIS prototype is constructed using a 3D printed framework and
characterized through measurements in free space and through a waveguide.
Experimental results demonstrate that the transmissive RIS is capable of
modulating incident incoming waves, producing 3.8 dB and 4.3 dB peak gains at
2.70 GHz and 3.00 GHz, respectively. The study also shows that the RIS exhibits
a high degree of phase sensitivity, with a phase sensitivity coefficient of 0.12
decibel per radian, which is in line with the theoretical sensitivity of a
rectangular waveguide. Ultimately, the study contributes to the development of
metamaterials, which is a crucial aspect of 6G wireless technology.

Reinforcement Learning with offline data has gained significant attention, and most previous research focused on the scenario with simple function estimation methods. However, little is known about the broader application of methods in this context when dealing with more complex estimators like decision trees or neural networks. This paper re-examines the underlying structure of offline RL under these more general conditions, thereby uncovering a fundamental linear optimization problem that underlies various existing non-parametric offline RL algorithms. This discovery also allows for a more comprehensive understanding of how the performance of these algorithms is influenced by several key factors, including data diversity, efficiency in extrapolation, and efficiency in exploration. Furthermore, this framework is utilized to develop a new theoretical model that accurately forecasts the performance of a sample-based proximal method for offline RL, and its effectiveness is validated through theoretical analysis and real-world testing.

We develop a straightforward and efficient method for building a continuous path in a higher-dimensional space without using a mechanical system that drives it. This approach is based on a geometric principle known as "free gift" or "gratis!" and allows us to track and follow the actual trajectory of two specific points as they intersect and merge. This is contrasted with the limitations of using traditional methods, which often result in artificial or artificially smoothed data. Our method is further adapted and applied to the task of creating a continuous path between two distinct points, or identifying specific points in a higher-dimensional space that correspond to given values in lower-dimensional subspaces.

Observations of the galaxy J0437+2456 have confirmed the presence of a massive, 
gravitationally bound system of 12 galaxies, with its center featuring a massive 
black hole. Our research indicates that the galaxy's central black hole is experiencing 
a turbulent state, with its effective mass fluctuating between 8.2 x 10^9 and 1.9. 
This instability is a result of the tidal interactions between the galaxy's surrounding 
matter and the supermassive black hole. As such, the galaxy's central black hole is 
expected to be a prime target for future studies on the gravitational waves produced 
by tidal interactions in galaxy centers.

Collinear four-point configurations in the planar n-body problem have received little attention despite extensive research on n-sided polygons formed by the points, which are either particle positions or rungs in the system. This paper examines collinear arrangements of three points at a specific time in the three-body problem, distinguishing between configurations that result in n-sided polygons and those that do not, and shows that the unique singularities in the problem, except for the collinear arrangement of the three particles at an equilibrium, are of the non-planar type.

Fluorescence lifetime imaging microscopy (FLIM) is a cutting-edge technique used to retrieve three-dimensional fluorescence lifetime images and intensity images of various samples simultaneously. The fluorescence intensity in FLIM is influenced by both the sample's optical properties and the detection system. As a result, the intensity is often distorted by the point spread function (PSF), which also affects the accuracy of measured fluorescence lifetimes. The proposed approach addresses this challenge by implementing an algorithm that corrects for PSF-induced distortions in the intensity and fluorescence lifetime measurements. The algorithm utilizes two-dimensional intensity and fluorescence lifetime maps of a standard sample collected before and after introducing distortions to correct for the effects of point spread functions of known shapes. The algorithm's effectiveness is demonstrated through simulations and experiments on biological samples and in vivo.

In e-commerce settings, personalized product search results depend heavily on users' historical interactions, which are frequently overlooked in current methods. These interactions encompass various behaviors such as clicking, adding to cart, and removing items. This paper introduces a novel user behavior model that captures long- and short-term user actions within a session to generate optimized search results. Unlike traditional methods, our approach views session interactions as a complex graph where nodes represent product actions and edges indicate temporal and semantic connections. We utilize a graph convolutional layer to derive actionable information from the graph. To overcome training efficiency issues, our model incorporates a spatial attention mechanism for data reduction and a graph pooling layer for hierarchical representation. We also incorporate a graph contrastive loss function to enhance representation accuracy. Experimental results on a real-world dataset demonstrate the success of our approach in generating more effective search results.

Graphs within the realm of machine learning and data science have emerged as a vital component in representation and analysis. Deep learning models are now integral to constructing graph embeddings, which are subsequently used for classification tasks. Embedding graphs as a vector allows for efficient modeling and is achieved by training a deep model on the graph's nodes, resulting in these nodes being mapped to lower dimensional spaces while preserving the graph's inherent structure. Despite the abundance of deep learning models, their reliance on labeled data poses significant challenges. This work delves into the realm of unsupervised learning, introducing a novel model called the Unsupervised Deep Manifold Characterized Graph Embedding (UDMCE) that leverages the structural properties of a graph to create node representations. This model is trained on the graph's shortest paths, which are inherently unique and serve as a proxy for structural characteristics. In contrast to existing models, UDMC-E does not require the computation of graph Laplacian, thereby reducing computational complexity. Our proposed model outperforms state-of-the-art benchmarks on real-world datasets, as evidenced by experimental results.

In two-way wireless sensor networks, granting access to devices is crucial, 
especially in Grant-Free Massive Connectivity methods, where a grant is not needed.
To improve the performance of this method, novel techniques, like Grant-Free 
Massive Connectivity, rely on non-orthogonal multiple access but face a challenge 
in designing sequences that maximize the probability of successful detection of 
active devices. To overcome this, we developed a two-stage genetic algorithm 
that generates a comprehensive library of sequence sets, enabling the system to 
select the most optimal one for its specific conditions. The results show that 
this approach significantly enhances the system's probability of successful 
detection and its overall efficiency.

Combinatorial compressed sensing is concerned with determining an unknown k-item set x its corresponding support from an m-dimensional frame H, where the coefficient vector y = Hz, in the presence of additive noise. Typically, this model relies on the assumption that the encoder matrix H is publicly accessible. This study explores scenarios where the encoder matrix is not available to either the decoder or the encoder. The latter scenario is referred to as the "encoder unseen" problem. The problem involves finding an iterative decoder algorithm for the "encoder unseen" problem that can recover the exact support with at most k errors, provided that the support is "well-separated" in terms of Euclidean distance (δ > 0) and the encoder matrix is well-structured (its columns have a Euclidean norm of D > 0). The proposed decoder algorithm achieves this with a high probability for large n and m values that satisfy the relationship n ≥ c_0 k log(k)/δ^2, provided that the generation process of H is uniform and well-structured for large n and m values.

Domain shift, a common occurrence in supervised learning, hinders the direct application of learned models to new data sets due to the mismatch in their underlying distributions. This often results in a significant drop in performance when tested on a different domain. Our focus is on the domain adaptation problem and developing a general algorithm that can effectively transfer models across such shifts, even in the absence of available target domain data. We achieve this by combining adversarial domain translation with stochastic transformations, demonstrating that this approach can successfully adapt models across various shifts, even those that are more complex and unpredictable. Furthermore, our algorithm can be incorporated into neural networks, allowing us to perform domain adaptation without needing target domain data. Our experiments show that this approach not only works well on simple shifts, but also on more challenging, non-stationarity shifts, and we also show its effectiveness in the more complex multi-domain learning problem.

This research paper focuses on 2-local and local derivations, as well as 2-local and local Jordan derivations on Jordan matrix algebras that are analogous to Weyl algebras, in the context of commutative, inversive rings. The primary outcomes of this paper include the demonstration of the existence of 2-local derivations, local derivations, and local Jordan derivations, which build upon a generalization of results initially established in [5] for polynomial rings. Furthermore, we identify and catalog the specific forms of 2-local derivations, local derivations, and local Jordan derivations that occur within these algebras.

We examine how Berry's phase arises from a system with a degenerate ground state, experiencing periodic driving, like a system with two energy levels. The system's Hamiltonian can be broken down into two components: one with a fixed periodic driving pattern and another, which varies randomly, and is set to zero. The fact that the system's ground state wave function is globally defined is due to the combination of these two components. A degeneracy in the system's ground state is removed when the system is driven periodically. A singularity in the system's degeneracy, which manifests as a singular Berry connection when the system is in its ground state, can be eliminated by the presence of the system's non-random component. This component effectively 'lenses' the singular Berry connection, allowing it to be eliminated by an observer. This phenomenon can be observed in various physical systems, including driven two-mode Bose-Einstein condensates and electronic systems with periodic driving.

We explore a unique scenario of a compacton forming in the center of a BEC when a spin-orbit coupling that varies with mass is introduced. We examine two distinct cases: one in which spin-orbit coupling is proportional to difference in mass, and another where it's proportional to the square of the mass difference. Through numerical simulation, we observe that the presence of the compacton is highly dependent on the initial state of the cloud and its size. We also find that the spin-orbit coupling behavior significantly influences the compacton's formation. Notably, in the case of mass-proportional coupling, compacton-like behavior emerges in nearly all initial states, whereas in the case of square-proportional coupling, it's primarily the smaller clouds that exhibit compacton-like behavior.

The quark spin symmetry dictates that the spin of the quark determines the spin of the hadron, provided that the quark's spin is conserved. Given this conservation, we examine whether the mass hierarchy of charmed baryons adheres to this quark spin symmetry principle by contrasting the massive counterparts of the $\Lambda_c(2595)$ with its less massive counterpart. A comparison of the known properties of the $\Lambda_c(2595)$ and its hypothetical massive counterpart, $\Lambda_c(2625)$, reveals a strong need for further experimentation to confirm the existence of the latter.

We denote L^2(G) as the second Chebyshev space, and consider a G-convolution symmetric Hilbert space H(G) containing L^2(G) as a subspace. We denote the primitive ideal space of G by $\overline{\mathfrak{X}}_{\pi}$, and assume that $\pi$ in $\hat{\mathfrold{G}}$ has a finite dimension. We denote the set of irreducible characters of G by $\hat{\mathfrold{G}}^{\mathrm{c}}$. We establish that if the set of irreducible characters of G is infinite, then H(G) is a subspace of a reproducing kernel Hilbert space associated with a continuous function on $\overline{\mathfrak{X}}_{\pi}$, and is equivalent to a direct sum of a Hilbert function space over $\overline{\mathfrak{X}}_{\pi}$ and a direct sum of a countable Hilbert space. We examine the production of Axion-Like Particles (ALPs) in the context of a high-energy muon muon collider. The collider would offer unique opportunities to study the couplings of heavy quarks with ALPs when compared to other accelerator facilities. Theoretical estimates suggest ALPs could act as a resolving mechanism to mitigate resonances that may appear in the future collider. We outline the theoretical framework necessary to investigate the ALP sector using muon colliders.

The increasing use of accelerators in data-intensive applications has led to a significant gap in efficiency between accelerator and inter-stage performance, with a growing need for cross-layer optimization to mitigate this performance imbalance. However, research and development of cross-layer optimizations face challenges due to a lack of infrastructure that enables their implementation, assessment, and comparison. In this paper, we introduce MetaSys, an open-source metadata management system, facilitating the evaluation of cross-layer optimizations in data-intensive applications. Metadata is crucial in optimizing application performance, but generating and managing it efficiently is difficult, requiring a system like MetaSys that leverages a domain-specific language to streamline the process. We propose four key aspects: abstraction, data management, scalability, and extensibility. We demonstrate the effectiveness of MetaSys through a case study using PyTorch and a range of accelerator optimizations, showing that MetaSys can efficiently manage metadata and optimize performance, resulting in speedup of up to 3.2x and a reduction of up to 75% in required metadata.

The recent development of transfer learning has significantly improved the accuracy of models in specific tasks. However, the conventional methods typically rely on pre-trained models to be re-used for new tasks similar to those the model was trained on. In this research, we propose an innovative approach using Siamese networks paired with a novel training strategy that enables the adaptation of models to various tasks. Initially, the model is trained to recognize pairs of identical images, and subsequently, the model is re-trained to recognize pairs of distinct images. This novel approach yields improved results compared to traditional transfer learning in image classification tasks, and its effectiveness extends to object detection and instance segmentation tasks as well.

In this paper, a comprehensive classification of quasilinear convective elliptic systems of higher order is provided, assuming suitable smoothness. Systems of this type that exhibit a unique solution for given boundary conditions over the entire space are identified, as well as conditions under which they possess a single, non-trivial steady state solution. Notably, these findings demonstrate that such systems are inherently non-isomorphic. Our research draws on previously established concepts, and extends them to a non-self-adjoint framework. The key results are organized into a hierarchical framework, allowing for straightforward verification of their applicability.

Neural networks struggle with capturing long-term dependencies due to vanishing or exploding gradients. Current long-term memory solutions, such as LSTM gates and convolutions, come with a computational cost. The paper introduces Fourier Recurrent Units (FRUs), a novel long-term memory approach that utilizes Fourier series to efficiently capture long-term patterns by transforming temporal data into frequency domain representations. FRUs outperform LSTMs in terms of accuracy and computational performance on the MNIST and TIMIT datasets, and a modified version of the FRU is presented. Furthermore, the paper introduces a long-term memory module that outperforms existing solutions like LSTMs and convolutions, achieving a higher accuracy on the TIMIT dataset while reducing computational complexity.

In a framework involving a decision maker and a fundamental environment, interactions are governed by a Markov process where the transition from one state to another depends only on the current state, and the decision maker's actions have varying levels of information complexity that impact the transition from one state to another. This results in a complex mapping involving a finite number of steps from an information set to a state transition. This paper focuses on an information set-based decision framework where partial observations are necessary, and the decision maker aims to optimize policy quality by minimizing expected costs at various information sets through the application of dynamic programming and the optimal backup plan method.

In this paper, we investigate the dual-wake injection technique as a potential method to generate highly brilliant and linearly polarized electron bunchs using a plasma radiator. The proposed method leverages two laser pulses that create electron emitters within the radiator, resulting in two distinct electron bunchs with synchronized temporal delay. Our analysis reveals that the injection of these two laser pulses results in increased electron acceleration and enhanced microbunching, leading to linearly polarized electron bunchs. Notably, this technique allows for the creation of highly brilliant electron bunchs even with a single laser pulse, and enables the generation of linearly polarized attosecond electron bunchs. Our results demonstrate the feasibility of this technique and provide insights into its application for the creation of linearly polarized radiation.

The universe's intricate nature raises the question of a potential link between life and cosmic complexity, which we investigate by exploring the concept of complexity in an abstract sense, especially in relation to living organisms. Our analysis involves comparing and evaluating systems with varying levels of complexity using a range of measures, ultimately discovering that these measures converge to reveal a hidden pattern underlying all living organisms. This hidden pattern, which we refer to as the Informational Hierarchical Structure (IHS), represents a potential key to understanding the origins of life. By examining the hierarchical structure found in the universe and its relation to the emergence of life, which in turn influences the universe further, we arrive at a model that we refer to as the "Biological Universe" model. This model suggests that life and cosmic complexity are interdependent, which we demonstrate using a simulation that tracks the development of life within a universe undergoing hierarchical development.

The climate crisis has led to a significant increase in global interest in research into climate change mitigation and adaptation strategies, making it essential to track the evolution of science and technology behind climate alteration efforts. To address this need, we developed a data extraction and classification framework from open scientific databases, which facilitates the creation of comprehensive datasets for policy-making, R&D, and infrastructure planning. Our study focuses on the evolution of climate alteration research in Spain from 2006 to 2020, using which we compared the effectiveness of artificial intelligence (AI) and human experts in assigning relevance labels to articles. The results show that AI outperformed experts in most cases, but human intervention is still necessary for cases requiring in-depth knowledge assessments. Furthermore, our findings are discussed in relation to R&D policy, highlighting the role of science transfer and international cooperation in climate alteration research.

The most widely used mobile operating systems, Android and iOS, remain vulnerable to a critical security threat - side-channel leakage. Despite Google's emphasis on security, its implementation in the Android Native Development Kit (NDK) leaves room for potential leaks in native applications, leaving developers to manually inspect their code for any possible leaks. This process, however, is time-consuming and requires a clear set of security guidelines. This paper proposes ASVAAN, a semi-automatic tool designed to evaluate the security of Android NDK applications, which can provide instant feedback on potential side-channel vulnerabilities while allowing developers to customize its functionality. ASVAAN not only extends existing tools but also adapts to the dynamic nature of modern software development, making it possible to integrate security checks into the daily code review process. This paper also presents the results of an experiment that involved 50 Android NDK applications, which revealed that ASVAAN can identify 95\% of side-channel vulnerabilities and correctly classify 96\% of other code segments as secure, thereby demonstrating its high accuracy.

This research delves into the study of ego networks within Ethereum's transactions. An ego network is established by an individual node and its immediate connections, each comprising a unique address on the blockchain, with accounts interacting with specific addresses for transaction purposes. By examining these ego networks, we can analyze transaction patterns, identify distinct user actions, and categorize accounts into various groups based on transaction types, such as YIN or YANG, to reveal different user behaviors. Our analysis explores the relationship between transaction fees, transaction complexity, and transaction types, with a focus on providing actionable insights to blockchain researchers and practitioners. Our study also proposes a novel method for categorizing user actions, based on the combination of transaction types and temporal features, which achieves a high accuracy of 92.2%.

The quantum fluctuations observed in low-temperature two-dimensional electron gases exposed to light exhibit a unique response to illumination. At temperatures below 1.5 K, the quantum fluctuations transform into distinct features when the electron gas is subjected to monochromatic light. These optical-induced features shift in relation to the frequency of illumination. Their characteristics can be manipulated by varying the intensity of the illumination, resulting in the emergence of multiple peaks. These optically-controlled quantum fluctuations have the potential to enable innovative methods for studying both the electron system and the effects of light.

In this paper, we examine the intrinsic relationship between the sequence category and Frobenius categories with commutative colimits. We show that sequence categories can be naturally derived from Frobenius categories with commutative colimits, and that the sequence category's adjunction with Pomset logic is a consequence of the Frobenius category's adjunction with its colimit category. Using this understanding, we develop both a unitary and non-unitary model-theoretic framework for pomset logic. Additionally, we explore the dual relationship between Frobenius categories and Lagrange categories with colimits, and demonstrate that the Lagrange category can be viewed as a subcategory of the category of coherent sheaves on the Grothendieck point. This perspective allows us to identify the standard topology on spaces derived from Lagrange categories.

The Ding-Iohara-Miki algebra has various generalizations of the Yang-Baxter and quantum Yang-Baxter identities to braids. These identities can be expressed using a fundamental $C_n$ monomial, with specific cases yielding the Fock and quantum group representations. We provide an additional polygon expression for the Ding-Iohara-Miki algebra, built on the $C_n$ monomial, valid for all polygons with seven or more vertices, and demonstrate that it fulfills the polygon identity in the Ding-Iohara-Miki algebra.

We have developed a system to calculate photometric redshifts for galaxies within two areas of sky: the Chandra Deep Field South and the ELAIS South-1 fields. This was achieved by combining data from various telescopes, including Hubble, the Very Large Telescope, and the Wide-Field Infrared Survey Explorer. We used a code called EAZY to calculate photometric redshifts for galaxies within these regions, relying on data from multiple bands in the observed spectrum. Our results were compared to spectroscopic redshifts for galaxies with known values, yielding an average error of 0.15 decimal places in the radio band and 0.02 decimal places in the optical band. We also identified and removed sources of error in the data, specifically in the VLT-VISTA band which was affected by a calibration error. This calibration issue led to a bias in the calculated redshifts, specifically an overestimation of values at 1 decimal place. We have developed a method to correct for this bias in future calculations.

To address the significant energy demands of China's projected population growth,
across various sectors, the country must consider both the "double constraints"
of "managing the economy" and "protecting the environment." Achieving a
sustainable energy structure is crucial, but it's hindered by the "prolonged
vacillation" of government policy uncertainty and path dependence. To provide
clarity and a clear path forward, a new decision assistance framework (DAF)
is proposed. This framework is grounded in modern Bayesian theory and offers
a transparent and reliable decision-making process for making energy policy
strategies. Its key benefits include: (1) the integration of human, material,
and information resources; (2) the capacity for continuous learning and
adaptation; (3) the capacity for "closed-loop" control; and (4) the ability to
optimize the "win-win" trade-offs between economic and environmental outcomes.
DAF's application in the energy sector can help to establish a sustainable
social, economic, and environmental framework, which is essential for
supporting China's "dual low carbon" goals.

We have established a fundamental result that establishes the optimal link dimension of two-electron wavefunctions expressed as matrix product states (MPS). Specifically, for a two-electron wavefunction expressed as an MPS at a given Hilbert space dimension $\chi$, we found that its link dimension is at most $3\chi$. This result significantly refines the previous bound established by Mitchell et al., which stated that the link dimension is at most $\chi^2$. We have also proven a more general result that optimizes the link dimension of general $d$-electron wavefunctions expressed as higher-dimensional versions of MPS.

We aim to address the anomalies in the muon and electron gaps, and our analysis reveals that the mass of the dark particle $\chi$, coupled with a specific $SU(2)_H$ gauge symmetry, significantly influences the $Z$-pole observables. The most plausible symmetry result is that $\chi$ has a mass of approximately $124.3$ GeV. The impact of the $SU(2)_H$ symmetry on the muon's anomaly is substantial, and it can be fully resolved by the model, whereas the model, with the same parameters, fails to adequately address the electron anomaly.

Digital twins, which combine a physical system with a digital representation, can integrate a physics-informed surrogate model to quickly generate accurate predictions. This approach involves a partial differential equation (PDE) solver and a physics-informed machine learning model, trained with real-time data from the physical system. Digital Twin Earth - Shores is an innovative digital twin that rapidly and precisely simulates coastal flood scenarios, leveraging a detailed solver and a physics-informed machine learning model. Trained on the STACOP tool's simulations, Digital Twin Earth - Shores predicts flood scenarios, water levels, and flow velocities, providing real-time predictions up to five times faster than traditional PDE solvers. This framework can be extended to various domains, such as medicine, finance, and environmental modeling, offering significant efficiency improvements.

BeyondPlanck and Cosmoglobe are two collaborative research initiatives, with the former focusing on gravitational wave physics and the latter on cosmology. Both projects center on open-source software development, data-driven research, and science outreach. They share a key objective - to foster an open and transparent research environment, promoting collaboration, education, and public awareness about scientific topics. The projects seek to establish a positive research culture by emphasizing reproducibility, data integrity, and durability - not just for the research itself but also for the software and underlying data. This article presents the history and evolution of the projects, delves into the underlying philosophy, examines the challenges faced in maintaining high research standards, and showcases the successful outcomes of science outreach efforts.

The emergence of spatial patterns in complex biological systems can be attributed to reaction-diffusion networks, particularly when triggered by an asymmetry in the medium. According to the Turing mechanism, patterns form when diffusion rates significantly differ from reaction rates. However, researchers have discovered that patterns can also arise when diffusion is reduced due to connectivity between interconnected sub-regions. While previous studies suggested network connectivity modulates the stability of these spatial structures, this study shows that transmission can actually induce instability, thereby promoting pattern formation. The findings, made possible through a novel approach to modeling interconnected reaction-diffusion systems, have the potential to expand our understanding of complex biological processes.

In a quasiclassical (or semiclassical) QFT, gauge fields are typically functions
of their own gauge invariant quantities. This is analogous to classical mechanics,
where physical laws are often expressed in terms of action variables. In a quasiclassical
Yang-Mills theory, the gauge fields should locally be expressible as gradients of
gauge invariant quantities. In this paper, we explore the conditions under which
this quasiclassical approximation holds in Yang-Mills theory.

In wurtzite semiconductors, the unique alignment of electrical currents within wire-like structures, known as quantum filaments, can be precisely controlled by manipulating their position in relation to the principle axis. An investigation into the dielectric properties of these filaments, using a technique that measures the dielectric response to monochromatic fields, has provided insight into their polarization effects. This method, known as THz-EOS, allows researchers to study the dielectric response of individual wires in a controlled manner, enabling the precise measurement of filament polarization within a diamond host. An examination of the dielectric response to monochromatic fields in relation to the chemical environment reveals distinct differences in the behavior of quantum filaments.

This paper focuses on learning the strategies of an opponent in the context of negotiation. We model negotiation as a joint Markov decision process, with the negotiation partner's best interests defined by a separate MDP that represents their objectives. We develop a method to create an opponent strategy model by analyzing the negotiation conversations of human counterparts and their associated preference models, and then test this approach using a large dataset of real negotiation experiments. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in predicting the opponent's future actions and their negotiation outcome, based solely on the current state of the negotiation.

In this paper, we explore the theoretical framework of D-branes with varying tension, considering a world-brane structure that interacts with the five-dimensional Anti-de Sitter space in light-like directions. We develop a detailed model that takes into account the cosmological constant on the brane and curvature of transverse space, and our analysis reveals that the background geometry can be influenced by distributional sources. We derive an equation that links the distribution density to a variable string tension, and our results show that the distribution density depends on the string tension's evolution. Furthermore, we examine the influence of distributional sources and variable string tension on both bulk and brane gravitational sectors, and our work provides a comprehensive understanding of distributional sources and variable string tension in gravity, valid in both string theory and general relativity.

The design of online sequential tests faces a key challenge of determining the optimal sample size for achieving accurate estimates of population parameters. To address this, we propose a novel online matching scheme, which balances sequential group testing for multiple subpopulations with distinct parameters. To evaluate the performance of this approach, we establish a metric that assesses the combined variability of estimates across the different subgroups. Based on this framework, we establish a sample size formula that remains valid under various scenarios, which we then apply to the SARS-Co19 antibody survey to estimate the antibody seroprevalence in New York City.

First-principles methods based on density functional theory are used to assess the accuracy of several dimer and surface models for the Si/Al2O3(0001)/Si interface. A comprehensive analysis is conducted to identify the most suitable interface configuration considering key criteria such as energy levels, interface electronic structure, and quantum mechanical/empirical potentials. This evaluation results in the identification of a "water-like" Si-O Si configuration as the most plausible interface model for the Si/Al2O3 interface.

We've developed a novel statistical method to analyze black hole collapse events, based on the Fitting Algorithm, which identifies the characteristics of gravitational waves through comparisons with modeled waveforms. Our approach focuses on the fundamental frequency of the collapse process. To achieve this, we've created a family of numerical solutions to the Einstein field equations, describing in-vacuo black hole formation from a rotating cloud of matter. Our results reveal that these collapses produce real-valued gravitational waves. Observing these waves leaves no indication of the cloud's angular momentum. Moreover, we've found that the Einstein quadrupole moment remains zero throughout the collapse. Additionally, we've determined that the gravitational wave amplitude is directly related to the total mass of the cloud.

The shipping industry, which is heavily reliant on market fluctuations in freight rates, attracts numerous investors seeking to capitalize on these changes. To gauge market trends and make informed investment decisions, it is essential to study historical freight rates and shipping volumes. Additionally, it is beneficial to compare the market values of different assets, such as newbuildings, second-hand, and scrap, which are often influenced by supply and demand. To address this need, we have compiled a comprehensive dataset spanning over 50 years, starting in 1966, consisting of freight rates, shipping volumes, newbuilding, second-hand, and scrap prices. To ensure the accuracy of our data, we matched the shipping volume data with available data on freight rates and shipping industry developments, such as newbuilding deliveries and second-hand ship deliveries and scrapping, and also verified the freight rates and shipping volume data against multiple sources. This dataset is now available for public use.

This paper delves into the strengths and weaknesses of various online anomaly detection methods, drawing a comparison between them, and assesses how effectively they can detect problems early on from log data analysis. Through our research, we identified a gap in the application of Hidden Markov Models for problem detection from log data, and to bridge this, we developed a framework that combines the strengths of various detection methods to offer improved results. This investigation aims to provide the necessary tools and concepts for the following paper, "Early Problem Detection from Log Data: A Comparative Study," which has been accepted for publication at the 2021 IEEE Network Operations and Management Symposium (NOMS 2021).

In the diagnosis of glioma brain tumors, accurate segmentation is a crucial imaging analysis tool that also enables detailed tumor anatomical models. A precise segmentation helps identify tumor cellular components, their cell density, and their local spread, ultimately guiding surgical approaches and helping assess treatment efficacy. Given the complexity of glioma segmentation, this study employed a recent Convolutional Neural Network model, designed to process large medical images, and demonstrated its effectiveness in a glioma segmentation task. Furthermore, this study introduced a computationally efficient post-processing technique to refine the model's output, achieving good segmentation quality. Our model was trained and tested using the publicly available BraTS2018 dataset, resulting in a high mean intersection over union score of 0.85, surpassing the performance of the official BraTS2018 challenge.

Research on magnetic materials, specifically magnetically ordered solids, has long been a focus in physics. Recent studies have concentrated on magnons, which are excitations within the magnetic background energy spectrum resulting from spin wave motion. Advances in handling low-temperature conditions have made it possible to conduct in-depth analysis on the properties of magnons. Advances in technology, including the creation of the first quantum magnonics devices, have enabled the production of high-quality samples under cryogenic conditions. Our investigation involves searching for evidence of the presence of triplons – a type of magnon trimer – in high-quality single crystals of the antiferromagnet MnF$_2$. Triplons are formed as a result of the merging of three spin waves and are a critical component in the theoretical structure of Heisenberg's antiferromagnet. To identify triplons, we conducted a thorough examination of the spectral structure near the magnon-magnon resonance in the temperature range where triplons are expected to emerge. Our findings indicate the presence of a peak in the heat capacity and the Raman spectrum, which we have observed at temperatures of 5.3 K and 5.7 K, respectively.

We introduce statistical convergence concepts that rely on a pre-determined direction, based on a modification of the concept of convergence governed by a modulus of continuity. The equivalence of statistical and strong convergence is also explored for a particular class of sequences. Furthermore, we examine the convergence properties of specific infinite matrices, in a context expanded from existing work, in the context of fuzzy numbers and sequences.

In this study, a noncontinuous Galerkin approach is applied to the one-dimensional Rosenau equation, utilizing a discontinuous Galerkin based finite element method. The solution is represented by a piecewise polynomial function, and we investigate two types of basis functions - the Taylor-Hood pair of $(\mathcal{P}_{k-1}\times\mathcal{P}_{k-2})\times \mathcal{P}_{k-2}$ and $(\mathcal{P}_{k}\times\mathcal{P}_{0})\times \mathcal{P}_{0}$, where $k$ is an even number. These basis functions, denoted as spaces $V_{1}$ and $V_{2}$, are used to approximate the solution. A noncontinuous Galerkin approach, combined with a weak enforcement of regularity through penalty terms, is used to derive the discrete scheme. The scheme is implemented using the Euler method for time discretization, and a conditionally stable explicit scheme is used. The convergence rate of the proposed method is demonstrated through numerical experiments.
