Deep neural networks have achieved significant success in image classification, but they often rely on limited training data from specific domains and struggle to generalize to unknown domains. To address this limitation, we propose a novel framework called IBDG that can effectively classify images from new domains even when no data from those domains is available during testing. Our approach combines a deep neural network with an interpretability-based domain discriminator that uses visual explanations to identify domain-specific features. We then use this domain discriminator to create a distributional estimate of the domain of a given image, which can then be used to adapt the network classifier to fit the target domain's characteristics. To further enhance the performance of our framework, we also propose a two-stage training approach. First, we train the network classifier using data from multiple source domains, and then we use the domain discriminator to produce an initial estimate of the domain distribution. We then select the image samples with the highest domain discriminator scores to augment the target domain's training set and perform an additional round of training. Our approach outperforms several other domain generalization methods in multiple benchmark datasets, even when no data from the target domain is available.

The Internet operates on a model of a closed, open, and dynamic infrastructure comprising various components, each serving distinct functions, such as the Internet Infrastructure, which includes the Internet, various devices, and technologies like IPv6, IPv4, DNS, etc. These components enable the Internet to function and are interconnected by Internet Components. The infrastructure's closed nature restricts communication beyond its limits, while its open nature permits interaction with external systems. Infrastructure domains are limited to communicating within their specified ranges, and collaboration between different infrastructure domains is essential for achieving their goals. To address this requirement, this paper introduces a collaborative agent that facilitates interaction between different infrastructure domains. Each agent is a blockchain-based system that enables communication, sharing, and coordination among various stakeholders. The paper's objectives are to introduce a new agent architecture, design a blockchain-based communication system, and propose a collaborative method that leverages the agents' capabilities. The proposed solution is validated through a case study, and the results indicate its efficacy in enhancing security, usability, and collaboration.

The $\alpha$-attractor PDB model, characterized by its potentials $V_0=V_0(e^{-\sqrt2\phi/M_P}+e^{-\sqrt2(1+\sqrt2)\phi/M_P})$, is a commonly used inflationary model that has been well-studied. In this model, $M_P$ is the reduced Planck scale and $\phi$ is the inflaton field, with $0<\alpha<3$, where $\alpha$ is a parameter that determines the number of local minima of the potential. When $\alpha=1$, the potential simplifies to the well-known Higgs potential, and when $\alpha=3$, it represents a special $\alpha$-attractor model. In this work, we investigate the inflationary configurations of the $\alpha$-attractor PDB model, particularly the end of inflation and the number of e-folds, and derive a general expression for the spectral index $n_s$ in terms of $\alpha$. Furthermore, we analyze the forecast of the Bayesian information criterion (BIC) and the evidence interval (EI) and find that they are consistent with Planck 2018 results for $\alpha$ in the range of $0.01\leq\alpha<3$.

This paper outlines a comprehensive framework for optimizing artificial intelligence (AI) workflows on Intel processors, as well as two innovative methods for enhancing neural network training and inference performance on Intel Xeon servers. The first method leverages data parallelism and a novel optimization technique to accelerate neural network training on Intel Xeon processors, building on the Intel Math Kernel Library for Neural Networks (I MKL NN) and Intel oneAPI toolkit. This approach is demonstrated through training ResNet-18 on ImageNet using up to 72 CPUs. The second method utilizes transfer learning and a hybrid approach combining CPU and Deep Neural Networks (DNN) libraries to develop a vision transformer model that achieves comparable performance to a ResNet-50 model. The paper also examines the efficiency of neural pipeline in inference mode and presents an alternative strategy for improving performance on high-resolution input images.

A recent study introduced a novel equivalence testing method, EquTest, which calculates the Bayes factor in frequentist procedures. We demonstrate that EquTest outputs can be accurately approximated using a logarithmic function, and this approximation closely mirrors the inverse relationships between Bayes factors derived from other equivalence testing approaches, including the log-HDI-ROPE and the Bayesian factor. This inverse relationship holds true across multiple scenarios, including direct and indirect EquTest outputs. To validate our inverse link function, we applied it to actual data from a comprehensive database, and our results indicate a high correlation between the approximated and actual EquTest outputs. Our findings suggest that any equivalence testing method can be transformed into any other, and this transformation is determined by the underlying data point values.

A new, semantic image transmission system has been designed, which uses a vector-quantized encoder to compress images and send them efficiently over an unreliable wireless channel along with a separate, coded sequence to guarantee accurate reception. The decoder, equipped with a decoder network, can recover the original images in color. The results of our experiments demonstrate that this method performs better than an alternative approach involving less information, while also being resistant to data loss even in the presence of high error rates.

As the global population expands, the sheer volume of data generated increases, necessitating the development of innovative analytical solutions that are both engaging and relevant to users' specific needs. This research paper explores the concept of an adaptive, result-oriented data analytics framework that not only captures users' interactions but also tailors its analysis in response, ultimately delivering anticipated outcomes. This study outlines a methodology for creating such an adaptive framework, accompanied by a comprehensive case study illustrating its practical application.

We examine the core concepts of category theory in the context of doctrines,
which are shown to be equivalent to Lawvere's theories, provided they have
appropriate structures. Specifically, we look at linear, biproduct and commutative
rigid doctrines, and translate their fundamental concepts - including monoidal,
pregroup and Frobenius adjunctions - in category - regarding the comonad as a form
of generalized adjoint representation. In order to formalize this connection, a
novel concept of a reduction is introduced. Furthermore, it is established that
every comonad is inherently linked to a pair of doctrines and their linked
structures, including the monoidal and pregroup structure on it, as well as the
bialgebra and a Frobenius adjunction.

A novel Bayesian nonparametric model is proposed to capture the dynamic behavior of interconnected networks, specifically within a network where clusters interact based on Markov processes. The model's structure is represented as a network, with relationships between clusters defined as a directed graph showing interactions between neighboring units. The proposed framework incorporates a two-stage hierarchical Bayesian structure, utilizing a Dirichlet process for clustering units, and a stochastic search process for modeling relationships between clusters. The method is then applied to a large dataset of electricity prices across different regions.

Current state-of-the-art document-level evidence retrieval models, which identify relevant evidence for a scientific question within a document, produce extensive annotations that guide training. However, generating such extensive annotations is costly and impractical for real-world applications. To address this limitation, we propose a new metric for evaluating evidence retrieval models and introduce RerrFact, a compact representation that condenses extensive annotations into a single, concise feature vector per token. RerrFact outperforms current methods in accuracy while reducing annotation time by up to 96%. We also introduce a new dataset, RerrFact-SCiSAR, which includes RerrFact features and extensive annotations, and demonstrates that fine-tuning BERT-based models with this new dataset significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art models, particularly in scenarios with limited training data.

We introduce an innovative automated system for categorizing and isolating posterior segment OCT images. This system leverages a hierarchical classification approach, combining machine learning with fast, flexible decision-making tools. A two-stage automatic classification system identifies specific OCT images, followed by a set of rules, incorporating deep learning, that precisely isolate and isolate the desired images, thereby achieving high accuracy and efficiency. This automated system is particularly useful in diagnosing and treating diseases related to the posterior segment of the eye.

Researchers have long sought to establish a clear understanding of human cognitive processes, but so far, no consensus has been reached. To shed new light on this complex issue, we present a groundbreaking approach known as neural superstatistics, which combines the principles of superstatistics and deep learning to model the human brain's cognitive functions. By harnessing the strengths of both statistical physics and machine learning, our new method, neural superstatistics, offers a fresh perspective on established theories such as global workspace theory and integrated information theory. Furthermore, our approach enables the computational simulation of cognitive processes, allowing researchers to experiment with alternative cognitive models and evaluate their effectiveness.

This research paper explores Mersenne primes, which is a subset of the famous Mersenne numbers with the form $M_n = 2^n - 1$. A Mersenne prime, in particular, is a type of integer that is both a Mersenne prime and a prime number; the known list currently comprises 49 such numbers. Notably, this paper will utilize an explicit expansion of the power function to establish a novel and innovative method for identifying Mersenne primes. Notably, this new method is capable of generating Mersenne primes with the given formula: $2^{p_1p_2...p_k}-1 = 2^{(\frac{1}{2}(p_1+\cdots+p_k+3))}-1$, where $p_1, p_2,..., p_k$ are distinct and positive primes of the form $4n\pm 1$. This formula is a direct outcome of the Binet-de Moivre's Theorem.

Hilbert's sixth problem involves understanding how smooth manifold-valued functions, defined through the behavior of particles in contact with a fluid, determine the fluid's behavior in accordance with conservation laws and dynamic principles. Researchers have developed various approaches to address this problem, including approximate methods, exact solutions, and mathematical proofs that confirm the dynamic principles' validity. The goal of this paper is to provide a comprehensive overview of these different approaches, which often overlap and complement each other. We begin by discussing the foundational mathematical concepts, continue with the study of fluid behavior around spherical and elliptical objects, describe the behavior of particles in a two-dimensional fluid, and conclude with the mathematical proofs that establish the dynamic principles' validity.

A universal correlation between the ratio of the stimulated to natural line widths of certain ionized and neutral gas emissions and the galaxy's star formation rate has been observed. This phenomenon suggests that galaxies with higher star formation rates have more efficient cooling processes, which can be attributed to the presence of denser gas reservoirs. The linear relationship between the stimulated to natural line widths and star formation rate has a slope consistent with the expectation of non-thermal emission processes occurring at subthermal temperatures. The average stimulated to natural line width of around 0.3 for the galactic neutral gas emissions implies that a substantial portion of the gas is at subthermal temperatures, which is below the critical density. This subthermal stimulation could be attributed to the presence of hot corona-like gas above the disk, which can emit natural C I lines through photon scattering. The existence of such a hot gas component may be crucial for the formation of molecular gas clumps and the development of star-forming galaxies.

This research paper outlines our efforts in creating a treebank for spoken language
data from the Klever project, where spoken Frisian and Dutch interactions are
documented. Our primary objective is to establish a reliable model linking spoken
language with written representations in the UD format. Due to a scarcity of
annotated spoken language resources, our proposed treebank will utilize code-switching
data that reflects the typical language behavior observed among Frisian-Dutch bilingual
children. The treebank will capture the transition between languages based on the
context, similar to adult speakers. Our proposed approach is a hybrid system that
combines the popular UD annotation style with insights from spoken language analysis,
event structures, and discourse grammar. The treebank will be developed in close
collaboration with the UD community to ensure seamless integration with existing
corpora.

The development of planetary systems is influenced by the evolution of the
protoplanetary disk, which experiences a significant change due to photoevaporation
around 4-5 million years after the star's formation. A critical factor in this process
is the star's mass. By examining the connection between the star's mass and disk
evolution, researchers can gain a deeper understanding of the formation of planetary
systems. In this study, we investigate the impact of a more realistic model of
photoevaporation on planetary core formation and the distribution of cores in
planetary systems. We find that stronger ultraviolet radiation emitted by more massive
stars accelerates the disk's evolution, resulting in fewer and larger planetary cores.
We also discover that the distribution of planetary cores in systems with varying
masses follows a power-law distribution with an index of approximately -1. This
finding suggests that more massive stars tend to have fewer and larger planetary cores,
whereas lower mass stars tend to have more numerous and smaller ones.

A collection of efficient three-dimensional numerical methods for simulating structural dynamics is presented, utilizing the finite element method and a generalized-$\alpha$ time integration approach with enhanced smoothing. The proposed methods are capable of accurately modeling complex wave phenomena and efficiently reducing numerical errors in frequency and time domain analyses. The performance of these new schemes is compared to established finite element time integration techniques and a novel $\alpha$-Gmres solver is employed to accelerate the solution of linear equations. The proposed methods are rigorously tested across diverse problem types, including statics, dynamics, and problems with changing loads, and are found to outperform conventional finite element time integration techniques in terms of accuracy and computational cost. The provided numerical results serve as a reference for future research and validation purposes.

We have examined the remnant decay rate of a polaron in a two-well Bose gas with a negative interaction using the semi-classical approximation. The decay rate is influenced by the properties of the ground state of the polaron and is notably accelerated by external noise. Notably, the decay rate is modulated by the frequency of the external noise. A resonance occurs around the frequency corresponding to the polaron's transition between its collapsed and trapped states. The decay rate is also affected by intra- and interband excitations, which modify the polaron's potential. The presence of these excitations causes a shift in the polaron's transition frequency and a significant decrease in the resonance amplitude.

Disaster relief logistics demands efficient and effective planning due to limited resources and the dynamic and uncertain nature of the supply and demand within the network. This study presents a stochastic programming model to address the dynamic constraints and adaptive decision-making processes. The framework includes a binary network design problem to determine the network structure, a continuous routing problem to determine the optimal route, and a quadratic cost adjustment problem to optimize the resource allocation process. The model's parameters are adjusted using a robust optimization technique to account for the uncertainty of the supply and demand. The computational results demonstrate the success of the proposed model in addressing the unique challenges posed by disaster relief operations.

The gravitational waves produced by binary supermassive black hole systems are the focus of this study.  The researchers investigate the gravitational wave signals emitted by binary systems with elliptical orbits, which deviate from circular orbits.  The team evaluates the accuracy of two methods used to model these waveforms: a simplified analytical model and a precise numerical model.  The impact of these waveforms on pulsar-timing array searches for gravitational waves is also examined.  The study's findings contribute to two key areas: they provide a reliable analytical model for computing gravitational wave signals, and they assess the accuracy of this model in detecting waveforms.  The study's main achievement is a precise numerical model for elliptical orbits in the post-Newtonian limit, which is essential for ground-based gravitational wave searches.  The model's accuracy is confirmed by comparing it to simulations of inspiralling elliptical binaries.  The study's results show that the analytical model is accurate for the first 20-25 post-Newtonian cycles, after which it becomes less reliable.  This finding is significant for gravitational wave searches that rely on such waveforms, particularly those using pulsar-timing array searches.  The study's results also show that the analytical model is accurate for computing signal power spectra, although the numerical model is required for precise power spectrum estimation.  The study's findings are crucial for gravitational wave searches that rely on such waveforms, particularly those using pulsar-timing array searches.

We're exploring the assumption that we have data from various games and the items placed within them, and we're investigating how to train a model so that it can predict the actions that players will take in similar game situations. To achieve this, we've developed a Watched Action Prediction Network (WAP-Net) which is a unique combination of a game's internal workings and the game environment. Our experimental results confirm that our WAP-Game framework along with WAP-Net effectively reduces the uncertainty surrounding potential player actions. Additionally, our WAP-Game framework also enables us to identify new game rules and player rewards, which in turn can lead to more efficient game AI development.

The terahertz region of the electromagnetic spectrum, spanning approximately 100 to 1100 GHz, is considered an ideal window for chemical spectroscopy due to the unique properties of its frequency range. However, the high absorption of water and other common liquids at these frequencies poses significant challenges for the development of terahertz communication and sensing technologies. To address this issue, our research team has successfully created a terahertz test environment that enables the in-depth analysis of water-based substances, including pure water, ethanol, and others. Our innovative on-chip measurement technique, based on the interaction between the sample and a high-quality, resonant silicon nitride cavity, has allowed us to study the complex spectral response of these materials with unprecedented precision and resolution. Our results, which cover the 750 GHz to 1100 GHz frequency range, demonstrate the potential of our method and will likely be used to advance the development of high-speed, high-quality terahertz communication and sensing technologies.

The COVID-19 pandemic has far-reaching effects on human health, with the World Health Organization (WHO) confirming over two million deaths and ten million reported cases worldwide. To combat this, a proposed project, AIRSENSE-TO-ACT, utilizes artificial intelligence to provide integrated support for both individuals and the community as a whole. By collecting data from various sources, including environmental monitoring, human activity, and health status, this project aims to provide a holistic understanding of the pandemic's impact and consequences. The integration of spatial data, machine learning algorithms, and data analysis enables the detection of emerging risks, allowing for timely interventions to mitigate the situation. Ultimately, the goal of the AIRSENSE-TO-ACT project is to provide actionable data to inform individual and community-level decisions, thereby reducing the human, social, and economic impacts of the COVID-19 pandemic.

In this research, we have developed a multi-phase, fluid-structure interaction model using the mesh-free, meshless smoothed particle hydrodynamics method. To model the interaction between a rigid structure and a two-phase flow consisting of an air bubble suspended within water, we have employed a combination of three different finite element and smoothed particle hydrodynamics finite volume methods. The interfacial boundary conditions between the three different mediums are formulated using the Kelvin-Helmholtz instability model. To simulate the three-dimensional, multi-phase fluid-structure interactions, we have utilized a multi-scale framework that combines a finite element method with a meshless smoothed particle hydrodynamics method. The simulation results show that our proposed framework is capable of accurately modeling the complex dynamics of multi-phase flows and fluid-structure interactions at various length scales.

Topological insulators exhibit unique properties where they display protected boundary modes even under the most extreme conditions of disorder and interactions. These modes originate from a non-local relationship between space and momentum dimensions, resulting in distinct topological features in both dimensions. Although the topological features in space are well understood, those in momentum space are not as well understood. This review aims to bridge this knowledge gap by exploring the concept of nodal surfaces in momentum space. It delves into the underlying principles, classifications, and examples of such structures, as well as their robustness and applications. It further discusses recent experimental implementations in photonic systems and offers insights into emerging research areas.

The HEP Software Foundation's Study Group for Large Scale Computing requested a report on event generators for the second stage of the HL-LHC Computing Model. This study aimed to identify shared software requirements, assess their potential for widespread use among key HL-LHC computing centers, and estimate the support needs of these centers, all in order to determine the necessary event generator configuration for the HL-LHC. The event generator landscape has become increasingly fragmented, with multiple options and limited cooperation, and this report had to navigate these complexities while considering the unique demands of the HL-LHC. Despite these challenges, this study aimed to gather event generator information from all relevant parties and make an informed recommendation for the second stage of the HL-LHC computing model.

This paper explores the relationship between the $p$-mean $T_p^c$ and the $q$-mean $T_q^c$ that is defined using a $c$-invariant function, which also characterizes the connection between the $n$-mean $T_n$ and the $(n+1)$-mean $T_{n+1}$. The paper further examines specific $c$-invariant functions, which include $\log$ and $\log(1+x)$, and presents an example of a $2$-mean function $\sigma_c(x)$ for $c>0$, extending the work of Menger for $c=1$ in [9]. The paper also establishes that $\sigma_c$ is a positive operator on a Banach space $E$ and is injective, which leads to the definition of the space $E_c$ of $c$-means. The paper then introduces the $p$-invariant mean $T_p^{\ast}$ and proves it to be both injective and a positive operator, which also leads to the definition of the space $E_{p,q}^c$ of $c$-means. The paper further explores the invariance of a $c$-function of integration, which also characterizes the relationship between the $p$-mean and the $(p+1)$-mean, and finally, the invariance of a $c$-function

The outer galaxy's star-forming process remains a topic of debate, with the possibility of a yet unidentified, dense disk of dark molecular gas. This "ultra-galactic ring" could be a key factor in the rapid star creation in the northern outer galaxy region. Our research focused on the region of NGC 6829, where star formation is known to occur, and utilized 45m telescope observations of the CS 7-11 source. Our analysis, which involved fitting the observed spectrum to a model, revealed a broad feature consistent with the emission of hot gas. Our findings suggest that this feature is likely due to the emission of hot gas from a dense disk of molecular gas in the northern outer galaxy region. Our estimates indicate a mass of approximately 1.1 x 10^7 M_sun and a temperature of around 200 K for this disk. Our research supports the hypothesis that this dark disk plays a crucial role in the northern outer galaxy's high star formation rates. Our findings have significant implications for understanding galaxy formation and evolution in the outer galaxy region.

This research examines the labor market dynamics in a comprehensive economy where employees can either work or engage in entrepreneurship, with the latter influenced by the quality of services and input costs such as wages and capital. It's been demonstrated that this economy has a singular equilibrium. This finding stands in contrast to previous studies which suggested the presence of multiple equilibria in less complex models. Additionally, the analysis investigates the circumstances under which some potential equilibria are inferior to the optimal equilibrium, providing an understanding that's relevant to current research contexts.

We study active polar particles in conditions where their motion is disordered and three-dimensional. By accounting for $n_d$ degrees of freedom in the displacement along the polar axis, we derive a free-energy expression that describes the behavior of these systems up to the mean-field level. This expression is based on a model that connects the polar angle $\theta$ to the displacement difference $\delta r$, where $\theta \sim \delta r^2$. We find that the mean-field free-energy is characterized by various terms including harmonic terms, a term related to nematic order, and terms representing nematic-nematic clustering, nematic-cholesteric interactions, and a cholesteric wave. By analyzing these terms, we can determine the conditions under which different types of ordered phases emerge, including cholesteric, nematic, smectic C, columnar, and columnar-nematic coexisting phases.

Within a bag model framework, we investigated the semileptonic decay properties of doubly charmed baryons, specifically examining their form factors and transition form factors. We looked at two distinct decay scenarios - the decay of a charmed ground state into a light meson and a charmless baryon, and the decay of a charmless baryon into a charmed ground state or an excited state. Our analysis revealed that the inclusion of a vector confining potential between quarks led to a strong vector nature, which in turn influenced the results. We found that the inclusion of vector confinement led to a significant increase in lower excited state form factors, with the inclusion of vector confinement playing a more substantial role than scalar confinement in determining these states. Our study's results were then compared to existing experimental data, which showed reasonable agreement, although further analysis is needed to confirm the accuracy of our predictions.

This study introduces a novel task called human localization through embodied dialogue, requiring automatic determination of a human's location in a 3D environment based on conversational data and 3D scene context. To achieve this, we have developed a new dataset, MoMo, comprising two large 3D virtual environments, MoPE and Poperty, with over 200,000 samples each. Each sample includes a human's 3D position, audio signal, and visual observation. We also present a two-stage pipeline for solving this task, involving the development of a listening model capable of localizing the speaker based on audio and the application of a semantic model to generate a list of most plausible locations based on speech content. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed pipeline, and the MoMo dataset is available at https://momo.human-cs.ai.

This research introduces an automated Band Importance Factor (BIF) algorithm for selecting the most relevant frequency bands in vibration analysis of rotating machinery. BIF method is effective in identifying critical features within a feature band and can be used to select frequency bands. Two key characteristics, similarity and non-redundancy, are considered when defining a feature band important, as it demonstrates the presence of similar features and ensures that the features in each band are unique. BIF method calculates the BIF value for each feature band by evaluating the number of peaks per band per cycle per vibration signal. It then identifies the most crucial bands by analyzing the top 50 most important cycles across all cycles and bands using the vibration signals from different sensors. In this study, the BIF method is successfully applied to real-world data from a 5kW induction motor under various fault conditions to evaluate its performance.

We conducted an in-depth analysis of the superconducting states of CaTSi3 compounds, specifically CaIrSi3 and CaPtSi3, through the use of low-temperature, negative-field muon spectroscopy. This spectroscopy, known as field-dependent muon-spin relaxation, effectively isolates muons from external magnetic influences, allowing them to relax into a transient state within the materials. This relaxation process, dependent on a time constant, has been observed in both compounds, resulting in similar time constants. Notably, CaPtSi3 demonstrates a field-dependent behavior indicative of a power law, resulting from a two-dimensional Fermi surface influenced by a three-dimensional superconducting state. In contrast, CaIrSi3's field-dependent behavior is consistent with a single power law across all fields, resulting in an exponent of 2, suggesting a two-dimensional energy gap. This two-dimensional nature is further supported by a comparison of magnetic penetration depths measured via both thermal and magnetic relaxation rates. Notably, both compounds exhibit lower-than-expected magnetic penetration depths, resulting in large energy gaps. This is further confirmed by a comparison of specific heat and superconducting gaps, resulting in a 3 to 4 meV estimated gap width for both compounds.

We've introduced an innovative solution to efficiently tackle Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman Equations in high-dimensional spaces, overcoming the computational challenges associated with excessive data sets. Our method effectively sidesteps the "curse of dimensionality" by harnessing the principles behind sparse grids, thereby allowing high-quality feedback control systems to be created for complex Markov Processes and stochastic PDEs using the feedback kernel method. This novel approach, named Traits Methods, integrates the flexibility of finite difference methods with the sparsity technique, resulting in highly parallelizable algorithms that can handle nonuniform grids and adapt to different grid structures. Our method employs a multi-faceted approach, combining numerical upscaling, multi-scale analysis, and upscaling techniques to precisely solve the feedback kernel partial differential equation and obtain the feedback control function. Our numerical experiments have demonstrated the superiority of this method in efficiently solving the Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation in high-dimensional spaces, achieving results that rival or surpass those obtained with other methods, including finite differences, boundary control, and barrier control.

Recent advancements in quantum machine learning have demonstrated the potential
of leveraging quantum computers for highly innovative applications. This study
focusing on quantum classification explores the challenges posed by quantum machine
learning algorithms. We employ two distinct quantum machine learning methods,
quantum boosting and kernel methods, to develop a quantum classification framework
capable of classifying quantum states based on their properties. Our experiments
demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach by successfully categorizing
quantum many-body systems across multiple dimensions, utilizing a high-dimensional
representation of qubit systems.

The integration of controllable energy resources, like batteries and hydrogen production, and efficient use of existing energy infrastructure are being explored as a solution to achieve a low-carbon energy future by maximizing the use of these flexible energy sources. These auxiliary elements can be considered part of a complex network that enables the reconfiguring of energy paths through a process called path reconfiguration. A mathematical framework is developed to model this concept, which involves the creation of a multi-energy dynamical model. The model is then applied to a large-scale network to demonstrate its effectiveness in optimizing energy production and reveal the potential of various paths that can be activated. The study also shows that a management strategy based on iterative optimization can be used to achieve efficient operation and energy production and utilization.

The 2D filtration model is founded on the concept that a fluid's dispersion within a porous medium is influenced by the fluid's interaction with the medium's surface at multiple scales. This interaction leads to the fluid's sticking to the surface, followed by the fluid's release after a certain relaxation period, represented by the variable theta according to a specific distribution. This distribution is characterized by alpha, beta, and gamma parameters and yields the value of theta as a function of these parameters. The final step involves calculating the fluid's final position after a specified time, dependent on the initial conditions and parameters alpha, beta, and gamma.

Researchers employed a specialized 1H MRI technique to study heat transfer within a packed bed of gas and microparticles, with the particles heated by an external laser heat source. Key aspects observed included: (1) the MRI successfully captured the temperature development (less than 1 mm) within the bed over time, (2) the temperature gradient in gas was significantly greater than that in particles, and (3) the boundary layer thickness in particles was proportional to the square root of time rather than time. This study's findings contradict the widely accepted "particle heat diffusion length" theory, suggesting that heat transfer from particles is significantly enhanced by convection, and this research highlights the potential of rapid MRI for studying thermal properties of packed beds.

In superconductors like UTe$_2$, an unusual property, reentrant superconductivity, has been observed when certain properties are strongly influenced by randomness. Specifically, the effect of random variations in crystal structure and electronic properties near its superconducting state causes this behavior. We developed a theoretical framework to explain reentrant superconductivity in complex systems, considering both types of random variations. Our model shows that thermal fluctuations enhance the superconducting state in systems with varying degrees of random instability, leading to unique phase diagrams. As a result, the superconducting state is improved by thermal fluctuations, which also explain recent experimental findings in UTe$_2$.

Recent advancements in ultra-wideband communication have been driven by the need
for short-range, high-accuracy measurements in emerging applications such as
industrial automation. In order to achieve low-latency communication, it is crucial
to optimize radio settings in real-time, factoring in factors such as distance
and interference. This research proposes a method for which a deep reinforcement
learning agent, trained in a simulated environment, adjusts radio settings to meet
the demands of specific applications. In this context, the environment represents
an application and its state reflects the surroundings and necessary settings. In
a simulated environment, the agent adjusts parameters such as the number of
chips, symbol length, and power to optimize a parameter that measures signal
quality. This approach has been tested using a UWB transceiver and has been
applied to real-world applications, yielding results that surpass the performance
of fixed settings and human experts in certain scenarios.

We investigate the semi-dynamic k-median clustering problem under different distance norms, namely Fréchet and Hausdorff distances. In this context, we consider a sequence of sets, each representing a point in a given metric space, and aim to cluster them into k non-empty groups such that the overall cost is minimized. For the case of discrete distance norms, we show that a polynomial-time algorithm can be applied to solve this problem, given that k is constant. Notably, this result holds in contrast to the continuous setting, where the problem is known to be APX-hard even under the Euclidean distance.

Multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) involves developing agents that collaborate or compete to achieve a shared goal through iterative learning. Despite the various algorithms used, they all face the challenge of obtaining a stationary solution to the MARL optimization problem. Building on the success of single-agent reinforcement learning, researchers have recently applied optimization methods to tackle MARL issues. This study focuses on a widely used algorithm known as Q-learning with double averaging in the primal-dual setting. Under standard assumptions, the analysis shows that this method achieves optimal results for Q-functions, while also demonstrating its robustness to various types of noise and its potential for application in scenarios with large state spaces.

Recent research has introduced coalgebraic satisfaction verification (CSV) as a $\mu$-calculus-based verification method that builds upon the logical connection between the coalgebraic semantics of programming languages and the Kronecker approximation. This work presents a coalgebraic framework for verifying the satisfaction of (probabilistic) $\mu$-program behaviors against (probabilistic) system behaviors. It specifically focuses on probabilistic $\mu$-programs running on probabilistic $\mu$-trees and systems represented by Markov decision processes (MDPs). Key findings include developing CSV adaptations for probabilistic $\mu$-trees, establishing the CSV-constructibility of basic system properties, and defining a CSV-based approximation method that converges to the coalgebraic semantics when the Kronecker approximation of the system converges to the system itself.

We propose a novel method to reconstruct the initial state of an evolution equation directly from a complete measurement data set. This involves using a reduced rank approximation of the initial condition, represented by a low-rank tensor that achieves the best fit to data within a given tolerance threshold. We investigate the existence of such approximations and develop a numerical method to estimate the optimal parameters, leveraging isogeometric analysis to evaluate the fit between the approximated solution and measured data. We assess the accuracy of our approach under various conditions, specifically when the initial condition is sparse, when data measurements are sparse, and when data samples are scarce. Through numerical experiments, we demonstrate the method's effectiveness in reconstructing sparse initial conditions from sparse and scarce data, and we discuss potential practical applications, such as reconstructing an obstacle from limited data measurements.

For the rapid growth of online-to-offline platforms, precise and efficient location-based services are essential. This involves constructing a comprehensive map of air conditioning facility locations and their energy consumption patterns, which can significantly contribute to energy conservation. This study develops a real-time mapping system using vehicle tracking data and proposes a new approach to a location-based energy consumption modeling problem. This involves creating a comprehensive map with minimal initial training data, achieved through a regressive model that estimates the location and consumption of air conditioning facilities based on vehicle tracking data and road facility detection information. Our solution utilizes a new dataset from New York City and demonstrates improved performance compared to existing methods in local and global prediction tasks.

We've developed a representation we call "Weil," which corresponds to a linear group derived from a ring composed of polynomials with a special type of involution - one that inverts the multiplication of its field, $R = \mathbb{Z}[\theta]$.
Here, the field $\theta$ follows a special type of polynomial transformation, where it represents roots of unity from a given power of a prime number, $p$.
Next, we created a second-class involution, denoted $\iota$, on $R$ which reverses the multiplication of its elements.
We then formed a representation we call $\mathrm{sgn}$, which corresponds to the given involution, denoted $\iota$, applied to a specific decomposition of the Weil Weil representation $\rho_{\mathrm{W}}$.
We've also developed a representation we call $\mathrm{std}$, which corresponds to the standard decomposition of the Weil Weil representation $\rho_{\mathrm{W}}$, using the given involution, denoted $\iota$, in the process.
We've further demonstrated that the given representations, denoted $\mathrm{sgn}$ and $\mathrm{std}$, are both unique, non-trivial, and orthogonal to one another.

The advancement of deep learning and computer vision has enabled the development of life-like and highly convincing video generation techniques. These methods, often referred to as video deepfakes, possess the potential to be both beneficial and detrimental to society. While they can be used for creative and positive purposes, such as realistic special effects in filmmaking, deepfakes can also be manipulated to deceive people and cause harm. This deception can take many forms, including, but not limited to, creating misleading video content, fabricating false evidence, and perpetuating hate speech. As a result, there is an urgent need to understand the underlying drivers of deepfake manipulation, identify the various types of convincing video content, and determine the necessary features for verifying video authenticity. This paper presents a unique survey focused on AI-driven video content that is designed to persuade. It begins by examining the key technologies involved in creating such content and discusses the various applications in which they are used to manipulate human perception. Next, it highlights the primary features of convincing video content and discusses the practical challenges associated with verifying video authenticity, followed by a comprehensive discussion of the related evaluation metrics in this field. Furthermore, this paper provides a detailed analysis of the current state-of-the-art research, future directions, and potential research opportunities in this field.

This research demonstrates the application of the hexapole trap as a motion compressor for ions. By utilizing this trap in conjunction with a set of equivalent linear traps, we mathematically formulate the motion compressed coherent states associated with the common linear potential and the hexapole potential. These states are then represented by applying the displacement operator to the ground state of the combined system. Additionally, we have formulated the motion compressed coherent states for a particle in a harmonic oscillator with a modified mass and an altered angular frequency. Furthermore, we have numerically simulated the behavior of the center of mass for a system of two calcium ions confined in a two-dimensional linear trap in the presence of a hexapole potential.

The increasing accessibility of powerful supercomputing systems has led to a significant growth in the adoption of numerical simulations for understanding complex biological systems, where the use of mathematical models is becoming more prevalent. Nevertheless, a major obstacle in the effective deployment of these models on supercomputers lies in the optimization of model-specific parameters to accurately replicate experimental data, a challenge further exacerbated by the intricate interplay between models and experimental settings, resulting in a vast multidimensional optimization space. This paper presents an innovative approach, which combines deep reinforcement learning and evolutionary optimization to efficiently explore the vast parameter spaces of neural models. We evaluate our method's performance on a specific neuroscience model, the cortico-basal ganglia model, and demonstrate its effectiveness on high performance systems, the JUQUEEN supercomputer in Finland and the Piz D'Arpino server in Switzerland.

We introduce a groundbreaking dataset, called Concealed Instance Segmentation (CIS), which poses a unique challenge in object detection, namely identifying objects hidden by other instances. To address this, we have compiled the CIS in-the-wild dataset, comprising 10k images with detailed annotations, collected from diverse sources, including the COCO dataset and novel natural scenes. Our initial attempt at solving CIS involves developing a multi-stage model that encodes, extracts, classifies, decodes, and refines object information. This approach is supported by a novel loss function and designed to complement existing object detection models through adaptation mechanisms. Our evaluation on the CIS dataset reveals the effectiveness of our proposed solution and our decision to make the dataset publicly available to foster further CIS research.

In this letter, we employ the two-fluid model of superconductivity, incorporating the effects of electromagnetic turbulence, to re-examine the possibility of violating the Lorentz force in superconductors. By combining the Lorentz force with mass movements within the two-fluid model, we develop a modified force model incorporating the influences of electromagnetic turbulence and the kinetic energy of superconducting materials. Our research reveals that the presence of electromagnetic turbulence can lead to a breach of the Lorentz force in superconductors. Furthermore, we establish a kinetic theory for the two-fluid model and, under specific conditions, demonstrate that the modified force model can be reduced to the standard Lorentz force model. Our findings suggest that the breach of the Lorentz force in superconductors is not an inherent property of superconductivity, but rather an emergent phenomenon resulting from the collective behavior of charged and neutral components.

As AI's presence in safety-critical environments such as self-driving cars intensifies, there's a pressing need to identify and rectify errors, especially those caused by machine learning.  Current methods for detecting and addressing errors, such as large-scale testing and controlled experiments, are costly and time-consuming.  This research introduces an innovative method for identifying and its verification of AI mistakes through crowd-sourced reports of errors.  Our approach capitalizes on the growing interest in crowd-sourced quality assessment and control to leverage collective knowledge to identify and rectify AI mistakes.  A novel system, AutoCrit, was developed to support this approach, which enables users to report AI mistakes and automatically verifies these reports through a range of methods, including controlled experiments and mathematical analysis.  AutoCrit has been successfully tested with various applications, including a popular language model, and has revealed AI mistakes that would have been difficult to discover through other verification methods.  AutoCrit has also been used to identify and verify AI mistakes in other areas, including image recognition and malware detection.  Our findings indicate that crowd-sourced reporting of AI mistakes is a viable and effective method for identifying and its verification of AI mistakes.  AutoCrit's availability as an open-source system enables other researchers to replicate and build on these results, which can be accessed at https://autocrit.github.io.

In object detection, a crucial decision-making process involves selecting the appropriate region of interest (ROI) from diverse proposals. Typically, a single-pass detector design relies on a fixed strategy, such as slicing and matching or sorting and sampling, which can be suboptimal. We propose a novel stochastic decision-making approach, R(Det)^2, which seamlessly integrates multiple passing methods to yield superior performance. By dynamically choosing the best passing strategy for each ROI based on its characteristics at inference time, R(Det)^^2 surpasses existing state-of-the-art performance, with improvements of 1.5% mAP and 0.5% nAP on MS-COCO and KITTI, respectively, and sets a new standard for region proposal passing.

Recent studies have shown that FGSM adversarial training can lead to overly precise models that incorporate unnecessary details from the data, resulting in poor generalization performance. This phenomenon is particularly pronounced when training condensed networks, and is closely tied to the complex structure of FGSM updates. In an effort to address these issues, we first examine the causes of overfitting and identify distinct patterns of noise growth during training. We then propose a straightforward optimization method, ZeroGrad, designed to harness the natural FGSM update momentum to mitigate overfitting. This approach can be easily integrated into existing adversarial training algorithms and is adaptable to a range of condensed networks. In contrast to alternative regularization methods, ZeroGrad provides a deeper understanding of the training process and is shown to consistently enhance performance, validate theoretical findings, and mitigate catastrophic overfitting caused by the backdoor attack.

We analyze the Thakurta metric, a hypothetical model proposed for developing event horizons in expanding universes. Our research reveals that this metric is infeasible for describing black holes; it doesn't satisfy established criteria like the Bondi-Metzner-Sachs condition. Additionally, we find that a static variant of the Thakurta metric exhibits pathological behavior, such as a singularity occurring at a distance from its center. Given these findings, we conclude that the Thakurta metric is not applicable to cosmological black holes. Consequently, our results indicate that restrictions on the masses of primordial black holes (PBHs) from LIGO-Virgo observations remain valid.

In recent years, many studies have focused on hybrid optimization techniques combining different algorithms to improve performance, but few have delved into the specifics of how changes in population contribute to this improvement. This study investigates the effect of periodically swapping assets within a particular class of hybrid algorithms, namely MaFEO, through a series of experiments. Building on the successful MaFEO, we developed a modified version called MaFEO-D that dynamically substitutes individual solutions in the population over time. Our analysis revealed a correlation between the improvement in the population and the quality of the solutions produced, showing which population manipulation is most beneficial. This research also aimed to establish a connection between the quality of the solutions and the diversity within a particular region of the search space. Our findings, however, suggest that existing metrics used to measure this diversity are not sufficient to guarantee a well-distributed population, thus highlighting the need for new approaches to assess the quality of the solutions.

A key advantage of fully homomorphic sparse evaluation (FFHE) type schemes lies in their ability to execute computations on encrypted data without decryption, while keeping results encrypted. However, homomorphic encryption generally incurs a significant performance cost. To mitigate this, our research proposes BTS, an efficient bootstrapping technique specifically tailored for use within the Cheon-Kim-Lee-Saikia-Waters (CKLS) system, as it is one of the fastest FFHE type schemes currently available. Our proposed method exploits the inherent properties of CKLS, leveraging its key pairing operation and BOSVAP gate to replicate RNS operations, resulting in an average 35% reduction in computation time compared to existing methods. By integrating this optimization, our homomorphic evaluation of the RSA key prediction problem on 192-bit RSA-2048, but with a 1,024-quadratic multiplication, can be executed in approximately 1,100 seconds. To further accelerate execution, our work also explores techniques to mitigate cache-related performance bottlenecks.

We have developed a set of randomly generated matrices based on the concept of creating a random ground-state configuration of N/2+1 fermions within a two-dimensional space with an adiabatic change in the energy profile from logarithmic to quadratic, resulting in a two-sphere-shaped droplet. By adjusting the strength of the external potential, we can control the size of the resulting droplet, allowing us to explore the transition between smooth density distributions and bumpy density distributions. By applying a series of exact transformations, we can map this system to a collection of N/2+1 harmonic oscillators with distinct frequencies, resulting in uniform density distributions for all N=1,2,3,...,infinity. We have demonstrated the effectiveness of our method by applying it to numerical data and verifying that it accurately reproduces the results, with an average error rate of 0.01.

Our research experimentally examines the concept of quantum connections, which describe the relationships between the eigenstates of a quantum system's observables. We have investigated these connections in a specific two-qutrit system, where each qutrit corresponds to a three-state vector. To do this, we measured the correlations and coherence of states that make up our experiment. To facilitate the measurement, we developed a method to generate pure states in a specific two-qutrit system, and we analyzed the measured data through various metrics such as the correlation function, entanglement, and relative Gell-Mann matrix coherence. Our findings show that the quantum connections in the eigenstates of the spin-1 total angular momentum and the $\hat{\sigma}_z \otimes \hat{\sigma}_z$ operator can be maintained with high precision. Importantly, we found that these connections are resistant to decoherence and can be preserved for an extended period.

The EPR argument's claim that a composite system's properties depend on spacelike- separated sub-systems leads Bell to conclude that local hidden variable theories cannot explain quantum mechanics. In response, we present a more flexible interpretation of EPR that makes hidden variable explanations possible again. Our approach, called decomposability, is based on a revised understanding of local realism that reflects quantum non-locality. This perspective, which aligns with the operational theory of local hidden variables, posits that a given property can be measured within a specific reference frame. As a result, different observers may have their own definitions of the property, potentially leading to contradictions when measured simultaneously by different observers. Our analysis shows that this new understanding of local realism can successfully explain the quantum theory behind correlations and entanglement.

We introduce StyleGAN-V, a versatile video generator based on StyleGAN-v, capable of efficiently creating high-quality videos with minimal computational and memory requirements. This advanced generator leverages a unique blend of temporal and spatial modeling, along with an adaptive multi-scale fusion technique, which can be implemented using pre-trained image models. By combining this approach with other innovative methods, including video embedding augmentation, progressive video training, and multi-scale video sampling, we have achieved significant breakthroughs in video generation. Notably, StyleGAN-V produces video frames at a rate of 30 per second using a single GPU, delivering a 10-fold improvement in speed. Moreover, StyleGAN-V outperforms other state-of-the-art video generators in both image and video evaluation metrics, while significantly reducing the computational requirements and memory needs of these models.

For connected complex reductive groups, we examine the differences in degrees associated with automorphic representations in relation to the generalized eta multipliers of Langlands. We also investigate the degree discrepancies of the original eta correspondence introduced by T. Gegenheimer for the cases of $SL_2(\mathbb{R})$ and $SO(2,N)$ as initially explained by Gross and Jorgensen via metaplectic language.

Deep learning has significantly improved the accuracy of dose estimation from patient-specific dosimetry when using whole-body thermoluminescence dosimetry (WBD) of the same recording. A comparison was made between two deep learning models: the conventional fine-tuning approach and a novel residual network. The study utilized 1,500 whole-body TL dosimetry records from the NPTLD database. The results showed that the residual network reduced uncertainty by nearly half compared to the conventional approach. Additionally, the study found that the residual network outperformed conventional fine-tuning models by nearly double for low radiation doses. The study also found that the performance of the residual network models increased with larger dataset sizes. The study demonstrated the potential of deep learning to improve dose estimation in whole-body TL dosimetry, thereby enhancing radiation protection and nuclear operations. The proposed residual network is expected to be integrated into clinical practice to estimate the date of exposure from whole-body TL dosimetry records.

This research paper investigates the existence and non-existence of solutions for a highly singular partial differential equation, specifically a double-stage parabolic system with singular and degenerate terms, on a closed manifold. The unknown variables are subject to nonlinear flux boundary conditions, and the problem employs a Sobolev space based on an arbitrary Orlicz function. Key findings include the derivation of Sobolev space embedding theorems in this context, along with the establishment of a maximum principle and the existence of weak solutions for the given problem under various conditions related to the exponents and the Orlicz function.

This research employs an FPGA-based Fastcat Circuit Board (FCB) to evaluate and compare the accuracy of simulated cone beam X-ray images generated by a phantom, under specific conditions including varying tube voltages and angles. We connected an FCB to a 3D printed cone beam X-ray apparatus and loaded a poly-echo water bath, allowing for the creation of absorption and attenuation maps. Two sets of measurements were taken at 120 kV and 20 MV, with and without the FCB attached. Digital simulations were conducted to model and confirm the accuracy of the measurements, with results showing a 98% match to actual experimental data. Notably, simulations accurately predicted attenuation within an error margin of 0.05% for both 120 kV and 20 MV cone beam X-ray simulations, with a similar level of accuracy achieved for a range of angles.

LIME is a widely adopted technique for explaining deep learning models, but its previous versions are prone to creating unrealistic "explanations" due to their flexible optimization, potentially resulting in inconsistent feature importance across multiple re-runs. To address this issue, our research introduces a new method called S-LIME that utilizes a unique sampling-based approach and is guided by a deep neural network to provide more stable and consistent feature importance across multiple evaluations. The results of our experiments using S-LIME on well-known image and text datasets show that it outperforms or matches the accuracy of previous LIME versions while offering improved explanation stability.

Machine learning models primarily focus on classification and regression tasks, but their capabilities can be expanded to provide more insights from training data. By implementing a just-in-time superresolution approach, researchers can analyze a model's confidence levels and the complexity of the loss function. This approach generates a secondary model that refines the original model, using a hierarchical approach that incorporates feedback loops. The refined model includes an additional layer that explains its predictions, and a training dataset that includes justification feedback. Through this approach, the enhanced model achieves higher accuracy and more accurate predictions compared to the original model, and the added layer provides more transparent predictions. The framework also allows for seamless integration of new classes, enabling it to become a self-adaptive model.

We have conducted in-depth investigations of TbInO$_3$ using high-resolution techniques,
including Raman spectroscopy and single-crystal Raman scattering, as well as optical
absorption and reflectivity. This work has provided detailed insights into the crystal-field
excitations and their corresponding symmetries, allowing us to establish a complete phase
diagram for TbInO$_3$. Our findings suggest that the phase diagram is characterized by a unique
ground state, which is stabilized by magnetic interactions in the crystal structure. The established
spectrum of crystal-field excitations in TbInO$_3$ is consistent with the material being a spin liquid
with a triangular structure, and our results offer valuable data for testing theoretical models of
TbInO$_3$'s behavior. Additionally, our analysis of the material's optical properties has allowed
us to deduce the effective crystal-field strength and the parameters of the spin Hamiltonian for
TbInO$_3$, which can be used to inform theoretical studies of the material.

We offer multiple solutions to an evolutionary problem in the realm of closed convex hypersurfaces within a complete Riemannian manifold occupied by non-negative curvature. This problem is defined by the non-linear partial differential equation associated with the power of mean curvature, specifically the n-th power of mean curvature evolution, given by $$\left\{\begin{array}{c} X_{\theta} \in \mathcal{H}^{2}_{|D|^{n-1}} \text{ on } |D|^{n-1},\\ \left. X_{\theta}\right|_{\partial M} = \mathbf{0},\\ \left. X_d X_d \right|_{|D|^{n-1}} = 0. \end{array} \right.$$ These solutions are derived by combining the principles of Gaussian and hyperbolic mean curvature.

A new approach to image convolution has been proposed, which replaces traditional convolutional layers in CNNs with an equivalent frequency-based operation. This transformation allows for the implementation of convolution within the frequency domain, leading to a significant reduction in computational requirements. As a result, models trained in this frequency-based framework can achieve faster inference times and lower memory consumption. A straightforward conversion method has been developed to transition existing CNN models to this frequency-based model, and initial experiments demonstrate that it yields competitive results across multiple applications, including image classification, object segmentation, and related tasks.

Recent advancements in deep neural networks have led to enhanced image grouping capabilities, but a significant limitation remains in the manual tuning of hyperparameters required for train-test validation, a process that becomes increasingly time-consuming and complex as network complexity and image size both increase. In an effort to address this challenge, a novel framework known as DeepCluE has been developed, incorporating a multi-layer ensemble approach that effectively aggregates the grouping information from individual layers within a network, thereby eliminating the need for individual hyperparameter optimization. Experimental evaluations conducted on the CIFAR-10 and ImageNet datasets demonstrate the efficacy of DeepCluE, yielding state-of-the-art results across multiple benchmark datasets.

The increasing occurrence of global crises has drawn attention to the need for effective risk management in complex socio-economic systems driven by human intuition and judgment. While our ability to recognize potential threats has been hailed as an asset, it is also a source of vulnerability. This research proposes a novel approach to addressing this challenge by establishing a universal framework for risk awareness, encompassing the identification of risks, their causes, effects, and mitigation measures. A unique method for representing knowledge graphs is developed to illustrate relationships between crisis types, incidents, preconditions, consequences, and preventive strategies. We also introduce a system for automating the analysis of news articles to forecast crisis occurrences and inform policymakers about impending risks, mitigating their impact through timely intervention.

Data categorization, a fundamental task in machine learning, involves assigning objects to pre-defined groups based on their properties. While machine learning algorithms have been successful in categorizing data, a critical challenge persists in creating an algorithm that can effectively learn a target variable's distribution. Research has shown that data's topological structure plays a vital role in categorization, and we propose that a well-constructed Voronoi tessellation around a set of reference objects can effectively categorize data. By examining the topology of these Voronoi diagrams, we can gain valuable insights into the distribution of the target variable. To this end, we introduce a set of indicators that quantify the topology of these diagrams, and demonstrate their effectiveness in a variety of categorization tasks. Through numerical and practical experiments, we show that these indicators enable accurate categorization, and we also demonstrate their interpretability in identifying clusters and decision boundaries.

This research paper explores an alternative approach for understanding contrasimilarity, a concept introduced by Choffrut and Poupet in [12], through the lens of game theory. Contrasting game theory with the partial order defined by contraction, we suggest a simple method for determining contrasimilar states. Building on this approach, we provide an answer to [12, Question 3.1] and demonstrate that states differing by a single contraction are indeed contrasimilar.

This paper aims to provide a comprehensive and formal definition of string 2-group, initially introduced in a paper by Jacques, one of the authors of this letter, published in 2007, and later developed in a paper by Schreiber, also one of the authors, published in a blog in 2017. The definition is rooted in category theory and framed within the foundations of homotopy type theory.

Numerical investigations into the ion-acoustic rogue waves in a system comprising double pair plasmas were conducted, taking into account non-extensive particle characteristics. Using the standard reductive perturbation method, non-linear ion-acoustic equations were derived and further simplified using the non-extensive moment method. This revealed that the rogue waves' electric field profile is influenced by the non-extensivity parameter alpha and the interaction between the two pair plasmas. This interaction can lead to the formation of rogue waves even when the two plasmas have equal densities. Furthermore, alpha was discovered to have a substantial impact on the rogue waves' profile. This research may lead to the development of a new method for generating rogue waves in laboratory settings.

A novel approach to analyze the Alfv\'en wave parametric decay instability in a plasma is proposed, which involves a two-way interaction between kinetic simulation and a two-mode two-variables normal mode expansion model. In this model, two variables represent the Alfv\'en wave and the decayed magnetoacoustic wave, with the former described using a kinetic simulation and the latter modeled using linear theory. The model's single-variable version, which only accounts for the Alfv\'en wave, is first validated against a two-variable model. It is then applied to study the ADWI and identify the most effective scattering plasma waves.

We investigate the impact of ambipolar diffusion within a magnetic filament on the development of gravitational instability, and the resulting structure. The filament is modeled as a thin, infinite sheet with a uniform density, extending from the surface of the disk into its upper atmosphere. The analysis focuses on the initial development of the most advanced mode, which leads to the formation of the initial column density structure. The study examines the relationship between the filament's properties and the resulting structure, with particular emphasis on the effects of ambipolar diffusion and the inclusion of magnetic field dynamics. The results show that the column density profile is influenced by the filament's atmospheric boundary, and the structure is divided into three sections: a region within the atmosphere where the field lines are vertically oriented, a section extending from the disk into the atmosphere where the profile changes non-linearly, and an area at the top of the atmosphere where the profile exhibits a uniform decrease in density. The study also reveals that the inclusion of ambipolar diffusion leads to a decrease in the Toomre quasistatic instability criterion by a factor related to the Alfvén travel time divided by the timescale of the field relaxation. The analysis provides a general expression for the initial growth rate of the most advanced mode, which is applicable to a wide range of field line orientations. The results are compared with observations of filament structures and the development of molecular clouds.

The application of repeated measurements on quantum systems has revealed the quantum Zeno and anti-Zeno effects, which have garnered extensive attention in past studies at quantum levels. Despite the significance of these phenomena, they have not been fully explored at macroscopic scales, especially in scenarios involving the repeated measurement of coherent superpositions of macrostates. This study aims to fill this knowledge gap by investigating the Zeno and anti-Zeno effects experimentally in a superconducting qubit repeatedly interacting with a cavity in the strong coupling regime. The findings demonstrate the Zeno and anti-Zeno effects occurring under these conditions, and provide further insights into their underlying dynamics, thereby contributing to our understanding of these phenomena and potentially opening up new avenues for their practical application.

We have examined the spin dynamics of a Heisenberg ferromagnet with Dzyaloshinsky-Moriya interactions in the presence of a homogeneous and inhomogeneous external field through the exact solution of a three-spin sublattice model. Our findings reveal that the inhomogeneous field's amplitude and direction have a substantial impact on the magnetization dynamics, particularly near the zero temperature limit. Moreover, the inhomogeneous field leads to a reduction in the maximum temperature at which a static solution exists and results in two separate spin excitation modes. Our analysis covers the relaxation of the spin component parallel and perpendicular to the initial magnetic field, demonstrating that the parallel component relaxes more quickly. Finally, the dependence of the spin correlation function on frequency and temperature was investigated, and the results were compared with the exact solution of a Heisenberg ferromagnet in an inhomogeneous field.

The movement of a swarm of drones can be defined by a set of interconnected nonlinear equations, but existing trajectory planning methods often fail to handle sudden changes in the group's configuration. To address this, we have developed a virtual distributed trajectory planning approach that ensures safe and feasible virtual corridors for the drones, preventing collisions within them. By defining the drones as elliptical shapes, we have developed a method to calculate a safe, virtual region within which the drones can move. We have also developed a control system that uses linear and nonlinear controllers to keep the drones within the safe, virtual region, by adjusting their speeds and directions to prevent collisions. Our proposed method is validated through both simulated and real-world experiments, and shows significant improvements in the performance and safety of the drone swarm.

Unsupervised Domain Adaptation is a key AI challenge addressed by unsupervised learning methods that transfer knowledge from a well-labeled source domain to a source task, using data from an unlabeled target domain. UDA has effectively solved complex problems in various fields like remote sensing, natural language processing, and computer vision. In this research, a new UDA benchmark called CARLANE is introduced, focusing specifically on lane detection, a fundamental component of autonomous driving. CARLANE features extensive datasets from simulation and real-world environments, encompassing diverse weather conditions, sensor configurations, lane types, and mapping styles. By applying established UDA methods, it's demonstrated that UDA effectively addresses the complexity of real-world data, ultimately enhancing lane detection performance.

Our investigation focuses on how the embedded volume fraction of poly(lactic acid) particles within a hydrogel impacts the static and dynamic contact angles observed between hydrogels and liquid substrates. By altering the embedded volume fraction, we're able to adjust the contact angle and, in some cases, induce a transition from a stable to an unstable contact configuration. Using a combination of high-speed imaging and advanced image processing techniques, we've observed a transition from a stable to an unstable contact configuration as the embedded volume fraction reaches a critical value. We've also determined the key factors that influence the static and dynamic contact angles using a numerical model based on a combination of the Lame and Laplace equations. Our findings suggest that the contact angle becomes increasingly unpredictable when the embedded volume fraction exceeds a certain value, making it challenging to accurately forecast the embedded volume fraction required to achieve a desired contact angle.

This research study tracks the correlation existing between the network connectivity of massive open online courses and the academic results of the participants involved, using data from a prominent MOOC provider. Building upon a previous study, this new investigation maintains a consistent evaluation framework while examining learners enrolled in courses during the COVID-19 pandemic. Given the unique circumstances surrounding the pandemic, this study aims to provide a more accurate representation of the relationship between network connectivity and academic outcomes. A comparative analysis is conducted to determine whether the pre-pandemic and pandemic periods exhibit identical relationships. Furthermore, this study aims to contribute to the existing body of literature on collaborative learning by investigating its correlation with academic performance.

A new, rapid wind profiling technique has been developed, which relies on 
vertical air path data obtained from an array of Doppler radar units, 
spaced about 5-10 km apart. This technique employs a specialized model to 
predict wind speed, utilizing even brief time series collected by the radar 
units simultaneously. The technique was tested using simulated data from a 
network of 6 L-band Doppler radar stations in the troposphere, specifically 
at altitudes ranging from 1 to 10 km above sea level. The results showed that 
even short data sets collected by the radar units within 2-7 seconds could be 
used to accurately predict wind speed, with minimal error, regardless of 
the specific conditions at different times.

UBC 274, a relatively young and compact cluster located at approximately 1.3 kiloparsecs away, shares some characteristics with the Hyades, including mean proper motion and spatial velocity. Using a combination of spectroscopic and photometric data from the Gaia Early Data Release 3 and archival data, researchers conducted a thorough analysis of this open cluster. They identified 19 candidate members based on their motion and color properties. These candidates form a distinct shape in the space defined by their proper motions and velocity, and their velocity vector points towards the direction of their galactic motion. UBC 274 exhibits a specific type of galactic rotation and a galactic Z-transformation. Its galactic plane rotation is opposite to that of the Sun, and its galactic Z-transformation is positive, indicating that the cluster rotates in a counterclockwise direction. UBC 274 exhibits a galactic rotation similar to that of other open clusters. UBC 274 exhibits a galactic Z-transformation similar to the Hyades and other open clusters. UBC 274 exhibits a galactic rotation-pressure profile that is consistent with theoretical models of galactic rotation. UBC 274 exhibits a galactic rotation-time evolution consistent with theoretical models of galactic rotation. UBC 274 exhibits a galactic Z-transformation-time evolution consistent with theoretical models of galactic Z-transformation evolution.
